In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

The disjointed letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'at) at the beginnings of the surahs of the Qur'an: sometimes one letter comes, such as (Qaf, Nun), or two letters, such as (Ta-Sin, Ha-Mim), or three letters, such as (Alif-Lam-Mim, Ta-Sin-Mim), or four, such as (Alif-Lam-Mim-Ra), or five, such as (Ha-Mim-'Ayn-Sin-Qaf, Kaf-Ha-Ya-'Ayn-Sad). Each of them has a key and secrets that have not yet been opened to us for knowing them, and what we have said about the meaning of these letters is merely attempts along the path.
"That is: what comes in this surah are the verses of the Clear Book."

Meaning: He recounts to you ﴿from the news of Musa and Fir'awn...﴾ [28:3]. The "naba" (news) is important information that deserves attention. And is there anything more important than the sending of Musa, peace be upon him, to the one who claimed divinity? For this reason this surah was devoted to the two of them, and no other mention appears in it except for Qarun, because it deals with the greatest matter, the matter of tawhid (oneness of God), and refutes those who claimed divinity and contended with Allah, exalted is He, regarding His attributes.

As for His saying ﴿with truth...﴾ [28:3], it is because its recitation and its narratives are true, as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, this is the true narrative...﴾ [3:62].

The word "qasas" (narrative) is derived from "qassa al-athar" (tracing and following a trail). Some of the Arabs were known for this in the past, and they excelled in it to the point that they could recognize the track of a man who had lost his camel. One of the trackers met a man, and asked him about it, so he said: "Is your camel short-tailed (abtar al-dhanab)?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Is it one-eyed?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Is it lame?" At that point the owner of the camel did not doubt that this man was the one who had taken his camel, so he seized him and brought him before a judge.

In the session of judgment, the man said: "By God, I did not take your camel. But I saw the camel scattering its dung behind it, whereas this one drops its dung once, so I knew that its tail was cut off. I saw that one of its feet did not leave an impression in the sand, so I knew it was lame. And I saw it eating from one side and leaving the other, so I knew it was one-eyed."

When Allah, blessed and exalted, recounts to us, He recounts the reality. The Qur'an's narratives do not know imagination as human stories do; for this reason He calls it "the true narrative" and "the best of narratives," because it recounts reality exactly as it happened.

Footnote 1: Al-abtar: the one whose tail (dhayl) is cut off, from any place in all animals; and al-batr: the severing of a thing by cutting. (Lisan al-Arab, root: b-t-r).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 28, verse 4:

The meaning of ﴿Pharaoh exalted himself in the land...﴾ (al-Qasas) is from "uluw" (elevation), i.e., he made himself high (istala). Those over whom he exalted himself were his subjects. Indeed, he exalted himself even over his ministers and the elite of his subjects, and he exalted himself until he even rose above Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and claimed divinity. This is the utmost of exaltation, the utmost of tyranny and arrogance. As long as these qualities are present in him, and he is a human being with desires, he will inevitably use them to humiliate his subjects.

﴿And made its people into sects...﴾ (al-Qasas). "Shiya" is the plural of "shi'ah," which is a group that has its own separate independence. In a kingdom, it is expected that the ruler treats his subjects equally, so that no class or group receives privilege over another. But Pharaoh made the people into groups, then set some of them against others and made some of them serve others.

There is no doubt that dividing one nation into several groups has a purpose for the one who does it. It is in his interest to sow discord among these groups and to occupy some of them with others, so that affairs do not settle among them and they do not have the leisure to think about what would worry him and shake his throne from beneath him, and so he remains the one sought by all.

The Copts were the inhabitants of Egypt and its basic race. Then, when Yusuf (peace be upon him) came to it and his affair became established until he was over its treasuries, and then his brothers came to take their provisions from Egypt, they settled there and multiplied, but they preserved their identity and did not dissolve into Coptic society.

Incidentally, many people err in thinking that "Qibti" (Copt) means Christian, and this is a mistake. "Qibti" means Egyptian as the basic race of Egypt. But when the Roman state colonized Egypt, and Christianity came with it, they applied the name "Qibti" to (Christian).

But what is the reason that Pharaoh made the people into groups, each enslaving the other? They said: because the Children of Israel were in the service of the colonizer who removed the rule of the Pharaohs, and they were the Hyksos kings (kings of the shepherds). When the kings of the shepherds were expelled from Egypt, it was natural for whoever ruled Egypt to persecute the Children of Israel, because they had been loyal to his enemies and walked in their train. From here came Pharaoh's persecution of the Children of Israel.

When the Noble Qur'an speaks of the kings of Egypt in the past and in recent times, it calls them Pharaohs, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Pharaoh of the stakes﴾ (al-Fajr, 10).

Here, in the story of Musa (peace be upon him), it also says "Pharaoh." As for the story of Yusuf (peace be upon him), no mention of Pharaohs is made; rather it says ﴿the king﴾ (Yusuf, 43). This is among the aspects of the inimitability of the Noble Qur'an, because rule in Egypt in the days of Yusuf belonged to the kings of the shepherds, and not to the Pharaohs, since the Pharaohs ruled Egypt before him and after him, when they recovered their kingdom from the kings of the shepherds. Therefore, specifically in the time of Yusuf, He said ﴿the king﴾ (Yusuf, 50). There was no Pharaoh in the era of Yusuf.

So the meaning of ﴿He oppressed a group among them...﴾ (al-Qasas, 4) is: a group, the Copts, who are the original inhabitants of Egypt, dominated the group of the Children of Israel, in order to take revenge on them for their loyalty to his enemies.

That is because the religion of Allah is one, and His commands are one for all. If you were adhering to the true religion, you would make people all one sect, such that some of them would not have temporal authority over others. So when you see in the nation this division and this partisanship, know that they are all indebted, because Islam, as we have said, in its purity is like water that has no taste, no color, and no smell.

This water everyone loves, and they cannot do without it to sustain their lives. But if we color this water with what we like, you love oranges, and I love mangoes, and this one loves lemons... etc. Then, desires have intervened, and the religion that Allah willed to be unified has become divided.

Therefore the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "My nation will split into sixty-odd or seventy-odd sects, all of them in the Fire except what I and my companions are upon" (1).

So the sect of Islam is one. But if we see on the scene dozens of factions, sects and groups, which one does the Muslim follow? Thus, since they have divided their religion and become sects, you have nothing to do with them.

Then Allah, the Exalted, explains this oppression: ﴿He slaughtered their sons and spared their women...﴾ (al-Qasas, 4). We have said that corruption is when one attacks the righteous in its very essence and corrupts it. So from corruption, then, is the killing of males and the sparing of females, because people's life is not sustained except by preserving the species. Killing males prevents the preservation of the species. He chose to kill the males because they were the source of evil for him, whereas the women had no power and posed no fear, so he spared them for service and for humiliation.

When we trace this verse, we find that it came in three places in the Book of Allah, each with a particular style. In the first verse, He, Exalted, says: ﴿And [remember] when We saved you from the people of Pharaoh, who inflicted upon you the worst torment, slaughtering your sons and keeping your women alive...﴾ (al-Baqarah, 49).

In another place: ﴿who inflicted upon you the worst torment, killing your sons...﴾ (al-A'raf, 141). These two verses are in the words of the Truth, Blessed and Exalted.

As for the other, it is a narration from Allah in the words of Musa (peace be upon him), when he enumerates the blessings of Allah upon the Children of Israel, saying:

﴿Remember the blessing of Allah upon you when He saved you from the people of Pharaoh, who inflicted upon you the worst torment and slaughtered your sons...﴾ (Ibrahim, 6).

The "wa" in ﴿and slaughtered...﴾ (Ibrahim, 6) did not occur in the speech of Allah, Exalted, but occurred in the speech of Musa, because he was in a position of enumerating Allah's blessings upon his people, and his intention was to magnify Allah's blessings upon them and to remind them of all the blessings. So he conjoined to ﴿who inflicted upon you the worst torment...﴾ (Ibrahim, 6) the phrase ﴿and slaughtered...﴾ (Ibrahim, 6).

But when Allah, Exalted, speaks, He bestows favor only with the essential thing, which is the killing of sons and the sparing of women, because the Truth, Blessed and Exalted, does not bestow favor with the small, but with the great. So the slaughter of sons and the sparing of women is itself the worst torment.

His saying once ﴿slaughtering...﴾ (al-Baqarah, 49) and once ﴿killing...﴾ (al-A'raf, 141) is because killing males took more than one form: sometimes they slaughter them, and sometimes they strangle them.

The meaning of ﴿inflicted...﴾ (al-A'raf, 141) comes from "sawm," which is for livestock to seek pasture, so we leave them to seek it in the open, gathering their sustenance themselves, not providing it for them ourselves; such animals are called "sa'imah." But those we tie and provide their food for are not called "sa'imah."

So the meaning of ﴿who inflicted upon you the worst torment...﴾ (al-A'raf, 141) is: they seek for you the worst torment, and since they are such, they must devise it for you in refined ways.

Then the Truth, Exalted, says:

1 Related by al-Tirmidhi in his Sunan (2641) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The Children of Israel split into seventy-two sects, and my nation will split into seventy-three sects, all of them in the Fire except one sect." They said: "And which is it, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "That which I and my companions are upon."

Therefore this oppression will not last for Pharaoh, because God, may He be exalted, has decreed that no wrongdoer (ẓalūm) prospers and that no wrongdoer dies until He takes vengeance on the wronged party from him and shows him in it the consequence of his wrongdoing, so much so that the wronged party may sometimes show mercy to the wrongdoer. And it is enough for you, as an example, a man whose envious rivals you saw yesterday becoming merciful to him today.

Here the wrath of the Truth, may He be blessed and exalted, confronts us on behalf of the believers: ﴿And We wished to bestow favour upon those who were oppressed in the land...﴾ (al-Qasas 28:5). The favour (minnah) is a gift given without any return and without effort on the part of the giver of the favour; it is as though it were a gift from the Truth, glorified be He, and a show of anger on behalf of His friends and the people of His obedience. For the Truth, may He be blessed and exalted, as the Imam ʿAlī said: "God does not abandon the truth, but leaves it to test people's zeal for it; if they do not defend it, He Himself defends it."

When the Truth, may He be blessed and exalted, becomes jealous for those who were oppressed, He does not merely lift the oppression from them, but also ﴿and We would make them leaders...﴾ (al-Qasas 28:5): leaders in religion and in values, and leaders in the governance of affairs and in kingship. ﴿And We would make them the inheritors﴾ (al-Qasas 28:5): that is, they inherit those who oppressed them and become masters over them and leaders for them. So consider through how many stages the jealousy of God comes to the people of truth.

Had Pharaoh, who grew strong over the oppressed and humiliated them, not been arrogant toward God and refused to submit, the mercy of God would have encompassed him, and he and his subjects would have lived as equals.

Therefore, those revolutions that came to put an end to the people of corruption and to secure justice for their peoples against those who oppressed them: after they have eliminated corruption, and after they have prevented the corrupter from corrupting, and have established justice in society, it was incumbent upon them to draw everyone into their embrace and care, so that everyone lives, after the situation has been set right, on equal footing within their society; and in this way we are secured against the counter-revolution.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66)) on surah 28, verse 6:

Then He, exalted is He, says, completing His favour:

﴿And We would establish them in the land, and show Pharaoh and Haman and their hosts from them that which they feared.﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We would establish them in the land...﴾ (al-Qasas: 6). We know that the land is a place in which events occur, since every event requires a time and a place. So the meaning is: We make the land a place in which they will be established. And "tamkin" (establishment, empowerment) means: they will dispose of it with authority and take its best.

The Truth, glorified is He, has explained tamkin to us in several places in the Qur'an. In the story of Yusuf, peace be upon him: ﴿Indeed, you are today with us established and trusted.﴾ (Yusuf: 54). "Makin" means: you have with us a standing and a firm position which no one can deprive you of in anything. Among them is His saying: ﴿And thus did We establish Yusuf in the land...﴾ (Yusuf: 21), meaning: We gave him authority by which he takes the best of the place, then distributes this good to others.

And His saying: ﴿And show Pharaoh and Haman and their hosts from them that which they feared.﴾ (al-Qasas: 6). Haman was the vizier of Pharaoh, and there must have been for each of them special soldiers distinct from the state's soldiers in general, just as we say now: the Republican Guard, the Royal Guard, and the army.

Or: Haman acted from within Pharaoh's inner circle, since a king does not conduct his affairs except through his viziers, and in this case the soldiers take their orders from Haman. Or: Haman had authority and a centre of power not less important than Pharaoh's authority, and perhaps he raised his head and overstepped against Pharaoh at some point.

We have seen this among us in Egypt, which is why they say in the well-known rural proverb, when someone tries to deceive you: "Are you telling this to Haman?" meaning: these tricks do not work on me.

The pronoun in ﴿from them...﴾ (al-Qasas: 6) refers to those who were oppressed, and ﴿that which they feared﴾ (al-Qasas: 6), meaning: We shall show them the thing they fear. What is intended is the prophecy that came to them, either through the soothsayers or through a dream, where Pharaoh saw a fire coming from Bayt al-Maqdis and dominating the Copts in Egypt, but not harming the Children of Israel. When they interpreted this vision for him, he said: There must surely come from this land someone who will snatch my kingdom from me.(1)

It is narrated that the soothsayers informed him that a boy would be born this year whose hand would bring about the end of your kingdom.

So Pharaoh and his people will see this matter with their own eyes and experience it themselves, and that which they feared will come to pass. Therefore Pharaoh ordered the killing of the male children of the Children of Israel, to take precaution regarding his affair and remain in his kingdom; but this precaution did not avail him anything.

1 Said by al-Suddi, as transmitted by Ibn Jarir al-Tabari and Ibn Abi Hatim; mentioned by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur (6/389).

Then the Exalted says:

﴿And We revealed to the mother of Moses: "Suckle him, and when you fear for him, cast him into the river, and do not fear nor grieve. We shall surely return him to you and make him one of the messengers."﴾ (28:7)

How strange is the affair of Pharaoh! After he ordered the killing of the sons of the Children of Israel, a chest carrying an infant at the breast comes to him on the river, and it does not occur to him that his family cast him into the river so that he might escape Pharaoh. How did this matter escape him, when he claimed to be a god? He would not have recognised it through his divinity, nor did he recognise it even through his cleverness and perceptiveness.

If the soothsayers had told him that the loss of his kingdom would be at the hands of a boy from among these children, and if that prophecy was true, then the boy must surely escape being killed and grow up and bring about the end of Pharaoh's rule. Since that is the case, Pharaoh would kill the children, but not the one at whose hands his kingdom would be lost.

The will of God decreed that Moses be raised in Pharaoh's palace, and that his poor mother come to him to live a life of luxury and wealth (1), and Moses, by the power of God, became a delight of the eye for the queen. Consider this dulling: a dulling of intellect and a veiling of the insight of Pharaoh, who claimed divinity.

Through this we understand the words of God Most High: ﴿And know that God comes between a man and his heart...﴾ (8:24). His heart covers his insight and blinds it.

As for His words to the mother of Moses: ﴿Suckle him, and when you fear for him, cast him into the river...﴾ (28:7). Which of women would accept, if she feared for her child, to cast him into the river? Who would be content to save him from a presumed death to a certain death? God Most High has made the tenderness of motherhood vanish before the inspiration of the Merciful that came to her, and which the inspiration of Satan could influence.

Then God Most High prepares also the wife of Pharaoh to complete this divine arrangement for Moses, so she says: ﴿The delight of the eye for me and for you...﴾ (28:9).

Pharaoh replies to her: "Rather, for you alone," as though he sensed what would happen. But the will of God must be executed, and destiny must take its course, nothing preventing it, for when God wills a thing, there is none to repel His will.

So despite what Pharaoh knew of the matter of the dream or the prophecy, he raised the boy in his house, and the matter is not free of the woman's control over the man in such a situation.

Therefore, when this verse was recited, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "By He in whose hand I am, if Pharaoh had said what his wife said, 'a delight of the eye for me and for you,' God would have guided him as He guided her" (2). It is only that he rejected the good that God had brought to him; therefore his wife embraced Islam and died in faith.

She it was who said: ﴿My Lord, build for me a house with You in Paradise, and save me from Pharaoh and his deeds, and save me from the wrongdoing people﴾ (66:11). As for him, he died in his disbelief, the worst of deaths.

We have already discussed God's revelation to the mother of Moses: ﴿And We revealed to the mother of Moses to suckle him...﴾ (28:7), and we said: revelation in the general sense of the language is informing by a hidden way, without your seeking out the one who reveals, or the one to whom it is revealed, or what is revealed. Legal revelation is God's informing His Messenger of a method for His creation.

God reveals to the angels: ﴿When your Lord revealed to the angels, "I am with you, so make firm those who believe..."﴾ (8:12).

He reveals to the messengers: ﴿Indeed We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him, and We revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob...﴾ (4:163).

He reveals to the faithful sincere ones in the service of a messenger: ﴿And when I revealed to the disciples: "Believe in Me and My Messenger..."﴾ (5:111).

He reveals to the bee, and even to inanimate things: ﴿When the earth is shaken with its shaking, and the earth brings forth its burdens, and man says, "What is wrong with it?" On that day it will report its news, because your Lord has inspired it﴾ (99:1–5).

Informing and revelation may also come from Satan: ﴿And indeed the devils inspire their allies...﴾ (6:121).

And it may come from the misguided: ﴿Some of them inspire others with ornate speech as deception...﴾ (6:112).

The revelation to the mother of Moses was a revelation of the fourth rank, by way of breathing into the heart, or inspiration, or a dream, or by an angel speaking to her; all of this is valid.

This revelation is from God, and its subject is: ﴿that you suckle him, and when you fear for him, cast him into the river...﴾ (28:7). This is a command ﴿and do not fear nor grieve...﴾ (28:7); a prohibition ﴿We shall surely return him to you and make him one of the messengers﴾ (28:7); and this is good news in two reports. So this verse gathered for the mother of Moses two commands, two prohibitions, and two glad tidings, in eloquent and miraculous brevity.

The meaning of ﴿suckle him...﴾ (28:7) is: for the duration of your security over him. ﴿And when you fear for him...﴾ (28:7) — it does not say "from what," to indicate any dread she might fear for her infant. ﴿Cast him into the river...﴾ (28:7). God Most High considers the feelings of the mother and her anxiety over her child, especially when she casts him into the river, so He reassures her: ﴿And do not fear...﴾ (28:7), because God will arrange for him an upbringing better than your upbringing under the shade of the house of the rich and the king.

﴿And do not grieve...﴾ (28:7), that is, for his separation; for this separation will compensate you, and will compensate the whole world with good, when He destroys this tyrant and His method comes to govern God's creation on earth.

Then know after this that God will return him to you, and make him among the messengers. So: I am the One who protects him, not only for your sake, but also because he has a mission with Me.

They say: the mother of Moses kept suckling him in her house as long as he was safe from the eyes of Pharaoh, until one of the watchmen came to search the house. She feared for the child, so she wrapped him in a cloth and put him into a niche beside her; this niche was the oven. She cast him into it while it was kindled (3), without her perceiving — that is, from the intensity of her fear for him — until, when the watchman had departed, she went to him, and found him safe, no harm having touched him. It is as though God Most High wanted her to be reassured of God's protection of him, and that His promise is true.

The matter of God's revelation to the mother of Moses has occurred in the Book of God twice, which prompted superficial orientalists to accuse the Qur'an of repetition without benefit, and they cited His words: ﴿When We revealed to your mother what is revealed: "Cast him into the chest, then cast it into the river, and let the river deposit it on the bank, and an enemy of Mine and his will take him." And I cast upon you love from Me, so that you might be raised under My eye﴾ (20:38–39).

But there is a difference between the first revelation and the other revelation: the first revelation concerns suckling during the period of security; the other, after she feared for him, was revealed to her to cast him into the river.

Consider ﴿Cast him...﴾ (20:39). Qadhf is casting with force, not placing with tenderness and gentleness, because God's care will protect him in any case. ﴿Let the river deposit it on the bank...﴾ (20:39). This is a command from God Most High to the river to bring the infant safely to the bank; therefore no mention of the act of suckling occurs in this revelation. So the first revelation came as a preparation for what would happen, so that the mother might be readied psychologically for this act; then the second revelation came for practice and execution, like a neighbour who tells you of something and warns you of thieves and advises you to take precautions in this matter, and when night falls the thing you warned of actually happens, and you cry out for him to hurry to them and strike them.

Therefore the style of speech differs in the first revelation, coming measured and reassuring: ﴿that you suckle him, and when you fear for him, cast him into the river, and do not fear nor grieve; We shall surely return him to you and make him one of the messengers﴾ (28:7). Thus it is in a calm tone, because the occasion is one of counsel and preparation, not one of events and execution.

But the second revelation comes swiftly, in a sharp tone: ﴿Cast him into the chest, then cast it into the river, and let the river deposit it on the bank...﴾ (20:39). The haste in the wording indicates that the occasion is one of direct engagement with the event itself.

In the first, He said ﴿cast him (fa-alqīhi)﴾ (28:7), whereas in the second He said ﴿cast him (fa-qdhfīhi)﴾ (20:39). A mother does not hurl her infant, but places him with tenderness and compassion; yet here the time is too tight to allow for the exercise of tenderness and compassion.

The command to the river to cast the chest onto the bank has its wisdom: the depths are the place of savage sea creatures from which one fears, whereas near the shore there are only small fish, which pose no danger; and also so that it would be in sight, so that his family would be reassured about him, and so that whoever would rescue him would see him, and he would reach the house in which it was decreed he be raised.

And indeed, the chest reached the shore, and Pharaoh and his wife Asiya and his daughter were on the shore. When they brought the chest out for them, they found in it the infant at the breast. Moses, peace be upon him, was dark-complexioned, frizzy-haired, large-nosed; that is, he was not, peace be upon him, handsome, so as to attract eyes and gladden whoever saw him.

Therefore He bestows favour upon him by saying: ﴿And I cast upon you love from Me...﴾ (20:39). That is, it was not by his own person that whoever saw him would love him, but by God's love (4). So when Asiya saw him, she loved him, and her breast was expanded by seeing him, and she clung to him despite Pharaoh's opposition to that.

Also, Pharaoh's daughter, who was a girl afflicted with leprosy (5), had seen in a dream that her cure would be by something emerging from the sea: she would take from its saliva and anoint the place of the leprosy, and it would be healed. When she saw Moses, she remembered her dream, so she took from his saliva and anointed her skin, and she was healed at once; thus she too clung to him.

So Moses gathered the love of the wife and the love of the daughter, and these two were in particular the holders of the word heard by Pharaoh, such that he would not refuse them any request.

In Pharaoh's submission to his wife's and daughter's desire, and his weakness before them despite what he knew of the child's matter, there is proof that the wife and children are a man's point of weakness, and a means of controlling his chivalry and resolve, and of pressing upon his wishes.

Therefore the Exalted reassures us about Himself, saying: ﴿He has not taken a consort nor a son﴾ (72:3).

That is because a consort often sways her husband by one means or another, while a son calls the father to cowardice and submission; but the Exalted has no centres of power that press upon Him in anything, for He is exalted above every deficiency.

They recount in the jests of Abu Nuwas that a man sought his intercession with the caliph Harun al-Rashid, so Abu Nuwas interceded for him, but the caliph did not grant his request, and the man waited to no avail. Then he thought of another mediation, and sought intercession with another at Zubayda, the wife of al-Rashid; when she spoke to him, he hastened to grant the man's request. Here Abu Nuwas became angry and reproached his companion al-Rashid, but he paid no heed to him, so he said to him: "Listen, then:"

The intercessor who comes to you clothed is not like the intercessor who comes to you naked.

And from this familial care for Moses, peace be upon him, we note that when his Lord said to him: ﴿Go to Pharaoh; indeed he has transgressed﴾ (20:24), Moses feared this mission, and the name of Pharaoh at that time struck terror into souls, to the extent that Moses and Aaron said: ﴿Our Lord, indeed we fear that he will hasten against us, or that he will transgress﴾ (20:45).

Therefore Moses asked his Lord for what would help him carry out his mission: ﴿He said, "My Lord, expand for me my breast, and ease for me my task, and untie the knot from my tongue, that they may understand my speech, and appoint for me a minister from my family, Aaron, my brother; strengthen through him my back, and associate him in my task, that we may glorify You much and remember You much; indeed You are ever Seeing of us."﴾ (20:25–35). Then what did his Lord say to him? ﴿He said, "You have been given your request, O Moses. And We had already favoured you another time"﴾ (20:36–37).

That is: you have been given all your requests and your aims.

1 Ibn Kathir in his tafsir (3/381, 382) mentioned: "Asiya, the wife of the king, summoned the mother of Moses and treated her well and gave her a generous gift, while she did not know that she was truly his mother, but because he had accepted her breast. Then Asiya asked her to stay with her and suckle him, but she refused and said: 'I have a husband and children, and I cannot stay with you, but if you wish I will suckle him in my house.' The wife of Pharaoh agreed to that and granted her provision, clothing, gifts and generous kindness, and Umm Musa returned with her child, content and pleasing, for God had replaced her fear with security, in honour, dignity and a house of provision."

2 Al-Suyuti cited it in al-Durr al-Manthur (5/569) from Ibn Abbas, and attributed it to Ibn Abi Umar al-‘Adani in his Musnad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Nasa'i, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh, and in it the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "By He in whose hand is my soul, if Pharaoh had acknowledged that he would be a delight of the eye for him, as his wife said, God would have guided him through it, as He guided his wife through it, but God, Mighty and Majestic, denied him that."

3 Sajara al-tannur yasjuruhu: he kindled it and heated it; it is also said: he gave it full fuel. (Lisan al-Arab, root s-j-r).

4 Al-Qurtubi in his tafsir (7/5137) mentioned that "some of the midwives entrusted with the pregnant women of the Children of Israel were friendly with her, and she said to her (the mother of Moses): 'Let your love for me benefit me today,' so she treated her, and when he fell to the earth, a light between his eyes overwhelmed her, every joint of her trembled, and his love entered her heart. Then she said: 'I came to you only to kill your infant and inform Pharaoh, but I have found for your son a love the like of which I have never found, so guard him.'"

5 Leprosy (al-baras): a skin disease that produces white patches on the skin that disfigure it, and it is one of the many symptoms of the disease of leprosy (judham). (al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/64).

6 Farrata 'ala al-qawm: he wronged them and exceeded the limit in ruling. God Most High said of Moses and Aaron: ﴿Indeed we fear that he will hasten against us, or that he will transgress﴾ (20:45), meaning: Pharaoh will wrong us and overstep against us. (al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/77).

Then the Truthful, glory be to Him, says:

﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a grief. Indeed, Pharaoh and Haman and their soldiers were sinners.﴾ [28:8]

Al-luqt and al-luqtah (lit. "picking up"): to find something without seeking it. From this comes al-laqit (the foundling), which is an infant nursling you find on the road without intending to, or searching for it. Likewise was the matter with the chest: the family of Pharaoh came upon it while they were sitting, not having sought it or looked for it, and as soon as they saw it they took it. But what was the reason for their picking him up?

The wife said: ﴿A delight for the eye, for me and for you...﴾ [28:9], and in another context she said: ﴿Perhaps he will benefit us, or we may take him as a son...﴾ [28:9]. They had no sons, so they wished him as a son for the daughter [i.e., for her], and she wished him as a medicine-solace (ṣaydalīyat ʿilāj, lit. "a pharmacy of cure"). But did this reason remain in place and actually come about?

No. They picked him up for another decree: ﴿that he might become for them an enemy and a grief....﴾ [28:8]. Not so that he would be a delight for the eye. The lam here in ﴿li-yakūna...﴾ [28:8] is lām al-ʿāqibah (the lam of consequence), meaning: they intended one thing, but the outcome brought something else.

In this there is an indication and a clarification of Pharaoh's foolishness and of the sealing over of his insight, despite his claim to be a god! After the soothsayers warned him, and after the dream he saw, and his knowledge of the danger this infant posed to his kingdom and to his life, he consents to raise him in his own house. This is the evidence for the truth of the words of the Exalted: ﴿And know that Allah comes between a person and his heart...﴾ [8:24].

As for the meaning of ﴿ḥazanan﴾ [28:8]: it means ḥazan, like ʿadam and ʿadam, suqm and suqm, bukhl and bukhl; so the meaning comes in both forms.

As for the words of the Truthful, glory be to Him: ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh and Haman and their soldiers were sinners﴾ [28:8].

They were sinners because their conduct did not accord with what they knew of the matter of the infant. They did not weigh matters, nor did they deduce the consequences. It was incumbent upon them to suspect the affair of a child who came in this condition; surely his people had intended to save him from the hand of Pharaoh.

The meaning of ﴿Comfort of the eye...﴾ (al-Qasas, 28:9). *Qarra* means to remain and to be settled. You say *qarra bi-l-makan*, meaning he stayed and remained in the place. From the same root, *qarur* means... *qarra* also means intense cold, as in the poet's words:

*Kindle the fire, for the night is a night of cold, and the wind, O boy, is a biting wind.*

*If you bring a guest, then you are free.*

So, the "coolness of the eye" is either its steadiness and absence of movement. The steadiness and settling of the eye is either physical or non-physical. Non-physical steadiness means that the eye rests on a sight or an object so that it is content and satisfied with it, and it no longer looks elsewhere.

From this comes the saying, "So-and-so has no other aspirations," meaning he is satisfied with what he has. Likewise, God Almighty said to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ):

﴿And do not extend your eyes toward what We have given to pairs of them as enjoyment...﴾ (Ta-Ha, 20:131)

Therefore, they call a beautiful thing that attracts the gaze, so that one does not look at anything else, "the fetter of the gaze" (*qayd al-nazar*). The poet says:

*My eye was fixed upon the moon, and it took from me by gazing.*

*Would that my blamer had an excuse, for its beauty is a fetter of the gaze.*

As for physical steadiness, it means the eye stays still in itself so that it does not see. From this is the woman's words to the caliph: "May God cool your eye and complete His blessing upon you." She seemed to be praying for him, but in reality she was praying against him, intending: "May God cool your eye," meaning: may He make it still and frozen through blindness. "And complete His blessing upon you": the completion of a thing is the beginning of its decline, according to the poet's words:

*When a thing is complete, its decline appears; await its passing once it is said to be complete.*

As for *qarr* meaning cold, it is known that heat by its nature spreads and disperses through a place. But God's wisdom broke this rule in the heat of the human body, as He gave each organ its own specific heat. The outer skin's natural heat stands at 37 degrees, while the liver, for example, does not perform its function except at 40 degrees.

As for the eye, if its heat rises by 9 degrees, it melts and the person loses sight. What is remarkable is that both are organs of one body. This is one of God's signs in creation. Therefore, when we pray for someone, we say to him: "May God cool your eye," meaning: may He make it cool and sound. Do you not see that when a person becomes angry, his eye heats up and his face reddens?

So the meaning here, ﴿Comfort of the eye for me and for you﴾ (al-Qasas, 28:9), means that it is a blessing and a pleasure for us, in which we rejoice and are content, so that we do not look at anything else.

In another place, God Almighty explains the comfort of the eye to us:

﴿God already knows those among you who hinder others and say to their brothers, "Come to us." And they do not approach battle except a little, being stingy toward you. But when fear comes, you see them looking at you, their eyes rolling like one overcome by death...﴾ (al-Ahzab, 33:18–19)

So these people's eyes roam here and there, just as we say: "So-and-so's eye is restless," meaning: it does not rest, whether from fear, anxiety, or agitation. All of this contradicts the comfort of the eye.

Her saying afterward, ﴿Do not kill him...﴾ (al-Qasas, 28:9), means that they had indeed intended to kill him. Thus, their minds were already set on the idea that Pharaoh's destruction would come at the hands of this child, and they were certain of it.

﴿Perhaps he will benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son, while they perceive not﴾ (al-Qasas, 28:9). This means they do not perceive whether he will benefit them or not, and whether he will be a son to them or an enemy.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 28, verse 10:

Then the True One, glorified is He, says:

﴿And the heart of Moses' mother became empty (of everything). Had We not bound fast her heart, she would have almost disclosed him, so that she might be among the believers.﴾

Al-fu'ad (الفؤاد): it is the heart (al-qalb), but the heart is not called fu'ad except when it contains matters that govern your movement. So the meaning is: "the fu'ad of Moses' mother became ﴿fārighan﴾ (empty)," that is, there is nothing in it of what regulates conduct. When she went to cast the infant away and remembered his separation and the dangers he would face, the feelings of motherhood nearly exposed her secret, and this emotion nearly carried her away.

﴿Inn kādat latubdī bihi﴾ (Had she not...): that is, she would have disclosed his matter.

﴿Law lā an rabaṭnā ʿalā qalbihā﴾ (Had We not bound fast upon her heart).

We have already said that a person perceives things through his instruments of perception, then this perception turns into feeling and emotion, then into inclination and action. We illustrated this with the rose that you see with your eyes, then you admire it, then you are inclined to pluck it, and at the point of inclination matters in the fu'ad confront you saying: "It is not right for you to do that; perhaps the owner of the garden will refuse or take you to court, for the rose is not yours."

Likewise Moses' mother: her fu'ad was empty of the matter that would reassure her about her infant, so that her emotions would not divulge this secret.

The meaning of ﴿rabaṭnā ʿalā qalbihā﴾ (We bound fast upon her heart) is: We made her firm, so that the matter became with her a firm conviction that does not float on the surface of emotion. Of this is His saying, exalted is He, about the People of the Cave: ﴿And We bound fast upon their hearts when they stood up and said, "Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth"﴾ (Al-Kahf 18:14).

So, binding upon the heart means preserving the matters that intervene in inclination: if it is not valid for you to do something, do not do it, and if it is valid, do it. These firm matters are what govern conduct, and the fu'ad of Moses' mother was empty of them.

Therefore we say to one who speaks empty words that have no meaning: "Leave off this empty talk," that is, what has no meaning and no benefit. Of this is their saying: "So-and-so's mind is empty," meaning that it lacks beneficial matters. Yet there is nothing that is completely empty; there must be something in it, even if it is air.

Of this is His saying: ﴿And their hearts are air﴾ (Ibrahim 14:43). And in colloquial speech they say: "So-and-so has nothing, not even air," because air is the last thing that can be emptied from a thing.

The meaning of ﴿Inn kādat latubdī bihi﴾ (she almost disclosed him): that is, her emptied fu'ad came close to saying, "He is my son" (2). ﴿Law lā an rabaṭnā ʿalā qalbihā li-takūna min al-mu'minīn﴾ (Had We not bound fast upon her heart, that she might be among the believers), because faith is what brings you benefit and keeps you from harm. Even if there is a hasty desire in something for you, her faith prevented her from the desire of motherhood in that situation, and from practising the natural tenderness and compassion of a mother, because this is a hasty desire followed by great harm: if they sensed that he was her son, they would kill him.

1 Several interpretations have been given of this word:
That is, empty of the remembrance of everything in the world except the remembrance of Moses. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Qatadah, al-Dahhak and others.
That is, empty of the revelation, since it had been revealed to her when she was commanded to cast him into the sea: ﴿Fear not and grieve not; We shall restore him to you and make him one of the messengers﴾ (Al-Qasas 28:7). This was said by al-Hasan, Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Zayd.
That is, empty of grief and sorrow, because she knew he had not drowned. This was said by Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Akhfash.
That is, her reason departed. This was said by Malik. The meaning is that when she heard he had fallen into Pharaoh's hands, her reason flew away from excessive anguish and bewilderment.
Al-Nahhas said: The soundest of these opinions is the first, and those who said it are more knowledgeable of the Book of God, the Mighty and Majestic. If she was empty of everything except the remembrance of Moses, then she was empty of revelation. Abu 'Ubaydah's saying, "empty of grief," is an ugly error, because what follows is ﴿Inn kādat latubdī bihi... lā an rabaṭnā ʿalā qalbihā﴾ (Al-Qasas 28:10). (Tafsir al-Qurtubi 7/5141)
2 Ibn 'Abbas said: That is, she would cry out upon casting him: "Oh, my son!" al-Suddi said: When she carried him for nursing and care, she almost said: "He is my son." It was also said: when he grew up she heard people saying, "Musa, son of Pharaoh," which grieved her and constricted her chest, and she almost said: "He is my son." (Tafsir al-Qurtubi 7/5142)

Then Allah, glorified is He, says:

﴿And she said to his sister, "Follow him,"¹ so she watched him from afar, while they did not perceive.﴾ [28:11]

Qaṣṣīhi (فصيه): meaning, follow his trail, and watch his movement to see where he went and what he did with him. When the sister heard this command, she hastened to carry it out; therefore the particle fa' (فاء), which indicates sequence and quick response, was used: ﴿fa-baṣurat bihi﴾ ("so she watched him"). It did not say "fa-qassat-hu" (so she tracked him), because baṣar (sight), although it means seeing, indicates care and attentiveness toward the thing seen.

The meaning of ﴿from afar﴾ (ʿan janb) is from a side such that no one sees her, and no one perceives her following him and her concern for him. Of this kind is what the Qur'an relates of the words of al-Sāmirī: ﴿baṣurtu bi-mā lam yabṣurū bihi﴾ ("I perceived what they did not perceive") [20:96], that is, he saw from a place where no one could observe him.

We note here that Moses' sister took the matter from her mother only as ﴿follow him﴾ and did not draw her attention to this precaution ﴿from afar﴾, which indicates the intelligence of the girl and her carrying out her task in the most complete manner, even though she had not been charged with that. This is from the wisdom of the sender who is keen to convey his message in its correct form.

How beautiful is what the poet said on this meaning:

If you are in need of a messenger, send a wise one, and do not instruct him.

Allah's words ﴿ʿan janb﴾ lead some to think that janb means "near me," and this is not correct, because the meaning of janb is that you are not facing me. Therefore He, exalted is He, says: ﴿and the neighbour who is near of kin and the neighbour who is a stranger [al-jār al-junub]﴾ [4:36]. So al-jār al-junub is the counterpart of al-jār al-qarīb (the near neighbour), meaning the distant neighbour.

From this is our saying: "So-and-so tajannabanī," or "So-and-so took the side (janb) away from me."

That is, he keeps away from me. Thus some understand this word in the opposite of its meaning.

Do you not see Abraham's words, peace be upon him: ﴿and keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols﴾ [14:35], and His saying: ﴿so avoid (fa-ijtanibū) the words of falsehood﴾ [22:30]? So ijtināb means keeping away.

And regarding the prohibition of wine, Allah says: ﴿Indeed, intoxicants, gambling, idols, and divining arrows² are an abomination of Satan's work, so avoid (fa-ijtanibūhu) it﴾ [5:90]. Then someone appears who says: "This is not an explicit text of prohibition, since it did not say 'it is forbidden to you'; it is merely an admonition and advice."

We say: if you understood the meaning of ﴿fa-ijtanibūhu﴾ [5:90], you would know that it is stronger in prohibition than "it is forbidden to you," because the meaning of "wine is forbidden to you" is: do not drink it, whereas ﴿ijtanibūhu﴾ means: keep away from it entirely, whether drinking, selling, buying, transporting, or even sitting in its gatherings.

¹ al-qaṣṣ: following a trace. It is said: "So-and-so went out qaṣaṣan in the track of so-and-so," when he follows his trace. (Lisān al-ʿArab, root q-ṣ-ṣ)
² al-azlām: plural of zalam, a piece of wood resembling an arrow with which they cast lots; they divide sacrificial animals by them, writing on each zalam a number, and whoever draws it from the gamblers takes the portion. It is a kind of gambling forbidden in the Sharia. (al-Qāmūs al-Qawīm 1/289)

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 28, verse 12:

Then the verses move on to the preparation of decrees for decrees, saying: ﴿And We had forbidden him the wet-nurses before, so she said, "Shall I direct you to a household that will rear him for you and that will be sincere toward him?"﴾ (12)

The prohibition (tahrim) here does not mean prohibition in relation to the obligated person (mukallaf), as in "this is lawful and this is unlawful." Rather, ﴿And We had forbidden him the wet-nurses...﴾ (al-Qasas 12) means: We prevented him from nursing from the women who were brought to him, so that the wet-nurses were turned over to him one after another, until his mother came to him.

And ﴿al-marad̲i‘* (al-marāḍi‘)...﴾ (al-Qasas 12) is the plural of murdi‘ (nursing woman, wet-nurse), and it is also said murdi‘ah. Each of the two words has its own meaning, contrary to what some think, that they have the same meaning.

Read the beginning of Surah al-Hajj: ﴿On the Day you see it, every nursing mother will be distracted from what she nursed...﴾ (al-Hajj 2).

Al-murdi‘ is one whose nature is to nurse and who is fit for this process, but al-murdi‘ah is the one who is actually nursing now, with a child at her lap sucking her breast. On the Day of Resurrection, this one will be distracted from her child because of the terror of what she sees. Thus, it is the nursing mother (al-murdi‘ah) who is distracted, not the one who merely has the capacity (al-murdi‘).

The pronoun in ﴿so she said, "Shall I direct you...﴾ (al-Qasas 12) refers to Moses' sister, because she was still engaged in the task of tracking the child. Haman heard her say, ﴿"Shall I direct you to a household that will rear him for you and that will be sincere toward him?"﴾ (al-Qasas 12), so he said to her: "You must be one of this child's family, and you know his story?" She replied: "Rather, they are sincere toward the king and devoted to him."(1) Indeed, they agreed with what she advised, because they were excused, since the child refused to nurse from the other women.

(1) Ibn 'Abbas said: When she said that, they seized her, doubted her affair, and said to her: "And how do you know of their sincerity toward him and their compassion for him?" She said to them: "Their sincerity toward him and their compassion for him is their desire for the king's happiness and their hope for his benefit." (Tafsir Ibn Kathir 3/381).

Then Allah, glorified is He, says:

﴿So We returned him to his mother that she might be comforted, and not grieve, and that she might know that the promise of Allah is true; but most of them do not know.﴾ [28:13]

Allah had already promised her: ﴿Indeed, We will return him to you...﴾ [28:7], and here is the time for the first promise to be fulfilled, which is good news of the fulfilment of the second promise: ﴿and We will make him one of the messengers﴾ [28:7]. But that is in the future of days, and it too will be fulfilled.

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿So We returned him to his mother...﴾ [28:13] shows that causes are in the hand of the One who causes, glorified is He. It is We who returned him, not his sister, nor Pharaoh, because We direct affairs in accordance with Our will, and We prepare the way for them, to the point that We come between a person and his heart, so that Our decree may take effect within it.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿but most of them do not know﴾ [28:13] means: they do not know that the promise of Allah is true.

Then the Truthful Lord says:

﴿And when he reached his maturity and was fully grown, We gave him judgment and knowledge. Thus do We reward the good-doers.﴾

Al-ashudd (maturity): this means strength and the completion of growth, and they have specified for it the age from eighteen to twenty. ﴿And was fully grown...﴾ (al-Qasas). Al-istiwa' (becoming fully grown) is the intellect reaching the stage of intellectual maturity. So when Musa (peace be upon him) attained the completion of bodily strength and the maturity of his intellect, ﴿We gave him judgment and knowledge. Thus do We reward the good-doers.﴾ (al-Qasas)

Then the Truthful One (Exalted is He) relates the account, saying:

﴿And he entered the city at a time of heedlessness of its people, and found therein two men fighting, one of his own faction and the other of his enemy. So he who was of his faction called for his help against him who was of his enemy, and Moses struck him with his fist and ended his life. He said, "This is of the work of Satan. Indeed, he is an enemy, a misleading adversary."﴾ [28:15]

Moses (peace be upon him) intended to enter the town at a time when its people were heedless, because the Children of Israel were oppressed, and the Copts in some of the densely populated cities would forbid the Children of Israel from entering their quarters. Therefore Moses chose the time when people were heedless; yet he did not enter at night, because he would not be guided to the road. It is said: he entered it at the time of the midday rest (al-qaylulah), when people were in their houses.(1)

﴿Found therein two men fighting, one of his own faction...﴾ [28:15] meaning: from the Children of Israel. ﴿And the other of his enemy...﴾ [28:15] meaning: the Copts. ﴿So he called for his help...﴾ [28:15] i.e., he asked him for aid and support. ﴿And Moses struck him with his fist...﴾ [28:15] meaning: he struck him with the full of his hands (bi-jam' yadayh). The Copt's end and his term came with this single blow, not that he died from it. This matter often occurs in a quarrel, for example between two people, where one strikes the other and he falls dead, and upon examining his body it becomes clear that he died from another cause.

An example of this: when you entrust a person with the fulfilment of a need of yours, or with intercession in some matter, and he goes to the officials and strives until they grant your need, you say, "So-and-so has fulfilled such-and-such for me," whereas in reality nothing was decided on earth except after God had decided it in heaven.

But God, exalted is He, wished to honour the intermediary, so He made its fulfilment coincide with His own decree, and in this case we say: God granted the benefit through him, not by him.

The Copts, as we have said, used to hate the Children of Israel and torment them. When Moses killed the Copt, their anger and hatred of the Children of Israel increased. Therefore Moses sensed that this deed was from Satan, who would increase this enmity: ﴿Indeed, he is an enemy, a misleading adversary.﴾ [28:15]

(1) Said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatadah. Ibn 'Abbas also said it, and in one narration from him: it was between the evening prayer (al-'isha') and the late night (al-'atamah). (Tafsir al-Qurtubi 7/5146).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 28, verse 16:

Musa (peace be upon him) teaches us that when a person commits a sin, and believes that he has sinned, he should not be arrogant. Rather, he should acknowledge his sin and his wronging of himself, and then hasten to repentance (tawbah) and seeking forgiveness (istighfar). ﴿He said: "My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me..."﴾ (Al-Qasas 28:16). That is: "O Lord, Your judgment is the truth, and I am the wrongdoer who acknowledges his wrong."

From here comes the difference between the disobedience of Adam (peace be upon him) and the disobedience of Iblis. Adam disobeyed, acknowledged his sin and admitted it, so he said: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves...﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:23). Then Allah accepted his repentance and forgave him. As for Iblis, he gave a reason for not prostrating: ﴿Shall I prostrate to one whom You created from clay?﴾ (Al-Isra 17:61), and said: ﴿I am better than him. You created me from fire and created him from clay﴾ (Sad 38:76). Thus he rejected the judgment of Allah.

Therefore, we say to whoever issues a fatwa other than what Allah has legislated, permitting the forbidden for some reason: beware of rejecting Allah's judgment, for if you do so, you are acting like Iblis when he rejected Allah's judgment. Rather, issue the correct ruling, and then, if you claim that circumstances do not allow its application, at least you keep your faith. Sin is erased by repentance and seeking forgiveness, but with disbelief there is no remedy.

When Musa sought forgiveness from his Lord, He forgave him. ﴿Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ (Al-Qasas 28:16). He knows the sin, and then forgives it out of mercy for us. For when a person is struck by heedlessness and falls into disobedience, if he finds no door of repentance and return, he despairs and loses hope, persists in his disobedience, and we call him "fāqid" (one who has lost hope) — he has an intense hunger for crime and no restraint against committing every sin.

Thus, the legitimacy of repentance and seeking forgiveness gives the believer hope that he will not be cast out from the mercy of Allah, because the mercy of Allah is vast and encompasses all his sins, however numerous.

Therefore, the Exalted says regarding the legitimacy of repentance: ﴿Then He turned to them in forgiveness that they might repent...﴾ (Al-Tawbah 9:118). The meaning is: He legislated repentance for them and urged them to it, so that they would actually repent and He would accept from them.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 28, verse 17:

Then the Truthful One (Exalted is He) says:

﴿He said, "My Lord, by what You have bestowed upon me, I will never be a supporter of the criminals."﴾

His words: ﴿by what You have bestowed upon me...﴾ (al-Qasas, 28:17) mean: by forgiveness, and by Your excusing me and accepting my repentance. ﴿I will never be a supporter of the criminals﴾ (al-Qasas, 28:17), that is: God has bound me by covenant never to be a helper of the criminals.¹

¹ That is: from knowledge, wisdom and monotheism. Al-Qurtubi said so in his tafsir (7/5148). Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir (3/382): "That is, by what You have granted me of rank, honour and blessing."

² He meant by supporting the criminals either keeping company with Pharaoh and being included in his ranks, increasing his numbers, when he would ride with his mount like a child with a parent, and he was called "the son of Pharaoh"; or supporting those whose support leads to sin and transgression, such as the support of the Israelite which led to the killing of the one whose killing was not lawful for him. (Al-Qurtubi in his tafsir, 7/5148).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 28, verse 18:

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, says:

﴿So he became in the city, fearful and watchful, when behold, the one who had sought his help the day before cried out to him for help. Moses said to him, "Indeed, you are clearly a misguided one."﴾

That is, after Moses killed the Copt, he became fearful of them ﴿watchful... 18﴾ (al-Qasas). He looks into the faces of the people, observing their reactions toward him, for perhaps they have come to seize him, as they say: "The guilty one almost says: take me!" If a group of people were sitting in a place and then the police suddenly confronted them, you would see them calm and fearing nothing, but the criminal flees running.

Among what the people of the countryside say about this is: "The one who has a bump on his head keeps touching it."

While he was in this state of fear and watchfulness, behold, the Israelite who had called for his help the day before ﴿cried out to him for help... 18﴾ (al-Qasas). Istasrakha means: he cried out, and called out to whoever would rescue him. It is an expression of seeking aid to escape a predicament. Among its uses is the words of God, Exalted, relating from Iblis: ﴿I cannot help you, nor can you help me... 22﴾ (Ibrahim).

We have previously discussed the hamzah of removal (hamzat al-izalah). We say: sarakha fulan means he sought help, and asrakhahu means: he removed the cause of his crying out. So the meaning of the verse is: I do not remove your cry, nor do you remove my cry.

Then Moses, peace be upon him, said to his companion who had put him into this predicament the day before ﴿Indeed, you are clearly a misguided one. 18﴾ (al-Qasas). He means: you want to lead me astray by having me do as you did yesterday. Moses, peace be upon him, would not fall into the same error into which he had fallen, for "the believer is not stung twice from the same hole" (2).

1 Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: he looks around from fear. It was also said: he awaits pursuit, and awaits what people will say about him. (Tafsir al-Qurtubi 7/5150) See also al-Durr al-Manthur of al-Suyuti (6/400).
2 A statement of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), narrated by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (6133), and likewise Muslim in his Sahih (2998), from the hadith of Abu Hurairah, may Allah be pleased with him.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 28, verse 19:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿So when he intended to strike the one who was an enemy to both of them...﴾ (al-Qasas 28:19). It means: Moses was moved once again against the man from his own group, who was the Israelite, and his helper. But this time the Coptic man confronted him: ﴿Do you intend to kill me as you killed a soul yesterday...﴾ (al-Qasas 28:19). He knew what had happened from Moses, and since they had come to know that he was the killer, they were bound to seek him out and take revenge on him.

And the words of the Exalted: ﴿You only intend to be a tyrant in the land, and you do not intend to be among the reformers﴾ (al-Qasas 28:19). Here "in" (إن) is negating: it means, you only intend to be a tyrant in the land. You killed a soul yesterday, and today you intend to kill me.

Then: they knew that Musa was the killer, and there had to be someone who would hurry to seize him. In this situation, a man of faith came running to him:

﴿And there came a man running from the farthest part of the city. He said, "O Musa, the chiefs are conspiring against you to kill you, so leave; indeed, I am to you among the sincere advisers."﴾

He is the believing man from the family of Pharaoh. He came to advise Musa to leave and flee before they seized him and killed him.(1)

(1) Most of the people of tafsir said: this man is Hizqil ibn Sabura, the believer from the family of Pharaoh, who was a cousin of Pharaoh. al-Tha'labi mentioned it. It was said: he is Ṭalūt, mentioned by al-Suhayli. Al-Mahdawi said, on the authority of Qatada: his name is Shim'un, the believer from the family of Pharaoh. (Tafsir al-Qurtubi 7/5152).
Because they persecute us and torture us without any cause, so what of it, now that they have found an opportunity and a pretext to increase their injustice against us?

Then the Truthful, glorified is He, says:

﴿And when he turned his face towards Madyan, he said, "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to the right way."﴾

The meaning of ﴿turned his face towards Madyan﴾: that is, towards its direction. He wanted to flee Egypt entirely, and he did not intend Madyan in particular; rather, he set out on a road which happened to lead to Madyan, the land of Shu'ayb (peace be upon him).

Had Madyan been his intended destination, he would not have said after turning towards it: ﴿Perhaps my Lord will guide me to the right way.﴾ For Musa, when he left Egypt in fear, wishing to escape, did not consider any specific destination. What mattered to him was that he leave this city and save himself.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 28, verse 23:

The Holy Qur'an presents this story in eloquent brevity, and despite its brevity it clarifies the role of the woman in her society, the role of the man in relation to the woman, and the necessity that compels the woman to go out to work.

The meaning of ﴿And when he came to the water of Madyan...﴾ (al-Qasas 23): he came to the water. Arriving (wurud) does not require that he drank from it. Wurud in this sense resolves for us the difficulty in His saying, ﴿And there is not one of you but will pass over it...﴾ (Maryam 71). The meaning is not entering the Fire and directly experiencing its heat; rather, it means going toward it and all of us seeing it. So: "we arrived at the spring," meaning we came to it and saw it, but drinking from it is another matter.

﴿He found upon it...﴾ (al-Qasas 23): that is, upon the water. ﴿A community...﴾ (al-Qasas 23): a group. ﴿Watering...﴾ (al-Qasas 23): that is, their livestock. ﴿And he found apart from them...﴾ (al-Qasas 23): meaning, away from the water. ﴿Two women driving back...﴾ (al-Qasas 23): that is, holding back their sheep and preventing them from drinking because of the crowding at the water. ﴿He said, "What is your affair?"﴾ (al-Qasas 23): that is, what is your matter?

In this interrogative there is the sense of wonder: why do you hold back the sheep from drinking, when you have come only for watering?

﴿They said, "We cannot water until the shepherds have dispersed, and our father is an old man."﴾ (al-Qasas 23)

Their saying ﴿until the shepherds have dispersed...﴾ (al-Qasas 23) means until they turn away from the water. Sadar (to depart) is the counterpart of warada (to arrive): the one who comes to the water is wārid, and the one who turns away from it is ṣādir. We say: ṣadara yaṣduru, meaning by itself (intransitive), and aṣdara yuṣdiru, meaning to cause another to do so (transitive).

So the meaning is: "We do not water until the people have watered and departed." And ﴿al-ru‘ā’﴾ (the shepherds) is the plural of rā‘in (shepherd). Then they mention the reason for their going out to water the sheep and undertaking the work of men: ﴿and our father is an old man.﴾ (al-Qasas 23)

Then Allah, glorified and exalted, says:

﴿So he watered their flocks for them; then he withdrew to the shade and said, "My Lord, indeed I am, for whatever good You send down to me, in need."﴾ [28:24]

So we have, in this story, three rulings. ﴿We cannot water until the shepherds have finished...﴾ [28:23] gave one ruling; ﴿Our father is an old man﴾ [28:23] gave a second ruling; and ﴿So he watered for them...﴾ [28:24] gave a third ruling.

These three rulings organize for the Muslim community the matter of women's work, and what is required of us when a woman is compelled to work. From the first ruling we learn that watering livestock is work for men. From the second ruling we learn that a woman does not go out to work except out of necessity, and that a man's task is not performed by a woman unless the man is unable to perform it: ﴿Our father is an old man﴾ [28:23].

As for the third ruling, it teaches the Muslim community, or even humanity in general, that if one sees a woman who has gone out to work, there must be no man to carry out this task for her; therefore it is incumbent upon him to help her and to make her task easy for her.

I recall that when I traveled to Saudi Arabia in the year 1950, I rode in the car of one of my colleagues. On the way, I saw him get out of his car, go to one of the houses, and there was a wooden table in front of it covered with a piece of cloth. He took it and put it in the car. Then we went on, and I asked him what he was doing. He said: "It is one of our customs that when you see such a table at the door of a house, it means that the owner of the house is not present, and that the lady of the house has prepared dough and wants someone to bake it. Whoever passes by takes it and bakes it, then returns the table to its place."

In His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We cannot water until the shepherds have finished﴾ [28:23] there is an indication that when a woman is compelled to go out to work, and this necessity is present, she must take the necessity only to the extent of its need. She should not mix with men, and should isolate herself from crowding them and rubbing against them. The fact that necessity has brought a woman out to perform men's work does not mean that she has become like them, permitting herself to mix with them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then he withdrew to the shade and said, "My Lord, indeed I am, for whatever good You send down to me, in need"﴾ [28:24]. Moses, peace be upon him, throughout his journey to Madyan had traveled without provisions, until hunger exhausted him and emaciation afflicted him until he became skin upon bone, and he ate from the herbs of the earth.(1) After he had watered for the two women, he withdrew to the shade of a tree to rest, and at that moment he uttered this supplication: ﴿My Lord, indeed I am, for whatever good You send down to me, in need﴾ [28:24].

It is as if the Truth, blessed and exalted, wants the weak to turn to assistance, and when he turns to it, he will not act by himself; rather, Allah will act on his behalf. Therefore we observe that Moses, in his call, said ﴿My Lord...﴾ [28:24] and chose the attribute of lordship (rububiyyah), and did not say "O Allah," because divinity (uluhiyyah) requires a worshipped one who has commands and prohibitions, whereas the Lord is the one who undertakes nurturing and care. So he said: "O my Lord, I am Your servant, You have brought me into this world, and I am hungry and want to eat."

The meaning of ﴿sent down﴾ [28:24] is that the good is truly from You, even if it comes to me through the hand of a servant like me; for when you trace any good in this world, it must end with Allah, the first Bestower. We have given as an example for this the loaf of bread that you eat: its beginning is a plant, which would never have grown without the care of Allah.

Therefore they say, in "al-Hamdu lillah" (All praise is for Allah), the form of generality within generality: even if you praise a person for a kindness he has done to you, in reality you are praising Allah, since every kindness ultimately ends with Him.

So, the praise of people is from within the praise of Allah, and praise in all its forms and all its directions, even if the causes return to Allah, Exalted is He. Some have said: "Do not thank Allah until you thank people."(2)

That is because the outcome of affairs is in His hand, Exalted is He, even if He has placed the causes in our hands; He, glorified be He, alone is able to nullify causes. I recall that some country (Pakistan) announced an abundance of wheat harvest, that it would suffice them and overflow for export; but before the harvest ripened, a calamity struck it and destroyed it, so all their calculations were upset, until they imported wheat that year.

This is the meaning of ﴿My Lord, indeed I am, for whatever good You send down to me, in need﴾ [28:24]: the good is from You, O Lord, even if You convey it to me through the hand of one of Your servants, and my need is only toward You, and my request is only to You.

Moses, peace be upon him, had barely finished his private supplication to his Lord when relief came to him: ﴿Then there came to him one of the two women, walking shyly.(3) She said, "Indeed, my father invites you that he may reward you for what you watered for us." So when he came to him and related to him the account, he said, "Fear not; you have escaped from the wrongdoing people."﴾ [28:25]

1. Ibn 'Abbas said: Moses traveled from Egypt to Madyan having no food except herbs and tree leaves, and he was barefoot, so that by the time he reached Madyan the soles of his feet had worn away; he sat in the shade, and he was the chosen one of Allah among His creation, and his belly was pressed against his back from hunger, and the greenness of the herbs could be seen through his inner body, and he was in need of a half date. (Tafsir Ibn Kathir 3/383)
2. Narrated by Ahmad in his Musnad (2/258), and al-Tirmidhi in his Sunan (1954), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever does not thank people does not thank Allah." al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a hasan sahih hadith."
3. 'Amr ibn Maymun said: She was not a brazen woman, going out and coming in. It was also said: She came covering her face with the sleeve of her garment, as stated by 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. (Tafsir al-Qurtubi 7/5157). The woman "salfa'" is the bold, forward one; and "salfa'ah" is the foul-mouthed, shameless one with little modesty. (Lisan al-Arab, root: s-l-f)

The commentary on His words, ﴿one of the two women﴾ (Al-Qasas 25), meaning: one of the two women, ﴿walking with shyness﴾ (Al-Qasas 25), meaning: bashful in her coming and bashful in her walking. ﴿She said: "Indeed my father invites you so that he may reward you for watering [the flock] for us"﴾ (Al-Qasas 25).

When this invitation came to him, he did not hesitate to accept it, and he seized this opportunity. He knew that it was a swift answer from his Lord to his prayer, ﴿My Lord, indeed I am in need of whatever good You send down to me﴾ (Al-Qasas 24). It is one of the means (asbab) that God extends to him, and it was not for him to reject the means of God. So he did not hesitate and did not refuse the father's invitation. The context here does not tell us how Musa and the girl went to her father, but it is related that they walked at a time when the wind was blowing from behind them, and the girl was in front, guiding him on the way. When the wind pressed her garment against her, describing her hips, he said to her: "O you, walk behind me and direct me to the way."(1)

This is another of the etiquettes of prophethood (adab al-nubuwwah), meaning the refined conduct that befits prophets.

﴿So when he came to him﴾ (Al-Qasas 25), meaning: our master Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, ﴿and related to him the story﴾ (Al-Qasas 25), meaning: what had happened between him and the Copt, ﴿he said: "Do not fear; you have escaped from the wrongdoing people"﴾ (Al-Qasas 25), meaning: he reassured him and calmed his fear.

1. Al-Suyuti cited it in al-Durr al-Manthur (6/405) and attributed it to al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, from Umar ibn al-Khattab.

This is a fourth ruling that we derive from these verses, taken from the daughter's words: ﴿O father, hire him; indeed the best one you can hire is the strong, the trustworthy﴾ [al-Qasas 28:26].

In her words is evidence that she did not desire to go out to work; rather, she sought someone who would do it in her place, so that she might remain settled in her home.

Then the daughter mentions the grounds for this proposal which she put to her father: ﴿Indeed, the best one you can hire is the strong, the trustworthy﴾ [al-Qasas 28:26]. These are two conditions that are indispensable in a hired worker: strength for the work, and trustworthiness in its performance. And you may ask: From where did the daughter know that he was strong and trustworthy?

They said: Because when he went to water their flock for them, he did not push among the people; rather he turned to another side and found there some herbage that he knew does not grow except near water. In this place he moved a large stone which cannot be moved except by a group of men, and then he watered for them from beneath this stone. She knew he was trustworthy when he refused to walk ahead of her, lest the charms of her body be exposed to him.

The father's role comes next, and the firmness that befits him in such situations. The man will be employed by him, and in his house are two daughters; he will be coming and going to them, night and day. Wisdom requires establishing a lawful bond for his presence in the house. Therefore he saw fit to marry him to one of them, so as to create a situation in which everyone may be at ease:

﴿He said: "I wish to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine, on condition that you serve me for eight years; but if you complete ten, it is from you. And I do not wish to burden you. You will find me, God willing, among the righteous."﴾ [28:27]

In proverbs we say: "Propose for your daughter, but do not propose for your son." This is because the pride of a father prevents him from presenting his daughter to a young man who has all the qualities of a righteous husband, although few people do such a thing. This wisdom on the part of the father in the matter of his daughter's marriage resolves many difficulties for us. We often find a young man who is sound in religion and good in character, but whose social standing, as we say, is below the level of the girl and her family, so he is too timid to approach her and is refused.

In this case the father must encourage the young man to come forward, and hint to him that he would be accepted if he proposed to his daughter, such as saying to him: "Why have you not married yet, my boy, when a thousand girls would long for you?" or other words of encouragement.

As for rising to the level of an explicit declaration, as did our master Shu'ayb, ﴿"I wish to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine..."﴾ [28:27] (al-Qasas), that is something else: it is a lofty courtesy regarding the offer and the one to whom it is made. In our societies many young men are waiting for this boldness and this encouragement from the guardians of the girls.

Do you not see that God permitted us to allude to marriage with a woman whose husband has died? He, exalted is He, said: ﴿"There is no blame on you for what you imply of a proposal to women..."﴾ [2:235] (al-Baqarah). And the allusive expressions that draw a woman's attention to marriage are not unknown to us.

As for His words: ﴿"on condition that you serve me for eight years..."﴾ [28:27] meaning: you shall be a hired worker for me for eight years. This is the bride-price of the girl. He intended by it to raise the value of his daughter, so that her husband would not say: "She is cheap," or that her father had thrown her onto him.

﴿"But if you complete ten, it is from you, and I do not wish to burden you. You will find me, God willing, among the righteous."﴾ [28:27] That is: when you live with me, you will find me good in dealing, and you will know that you were successful in this kinship; indeed, this period will increase your love for remaining with us.

1 Moses, peace be upon him, married the younger of the two. On the authority of Abu Hurayrah, who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Jibril said to me: 'O Muhammad, if the Jew asks you which of the two terms Moses fulfilled, say: the more complete of them; and if they ask you which of them he married, say: the younger of them.'" Al-Suyuti cited it in al-Durr al-Manthur (6/410) and attributed it to Ibn Mardawayh. He also cited something similar from a hadith of Abu Dharr and attributed it to al-Bazzar, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani in al-Awsat and Ibn Mardawayh, with a weak chain of narration.

Moses, peace be upon him, answered:

﴿He said: "That is between me and you. Whichever of the two terms I fulfil, let there be no injustice against me. And Allah is Witness over what we say."﴾ [28:28]

That is: I have the choice, whether I complete eight years or ten.

﴿Let there be no injustice against me, and Allah is Witness over what we say.﴾ [28:28]

The scholars have derived a new ruling from this verse: that at the contracting of marriage what is required is the naming of the bridal gift (mahr), and its delivery is not a condition at the time of the contract. You may defer all of it and make it deferred, or defer part of it and pay part of it.

The mahr is the price of the woman's womanhood (bud'), such that if she dies it passes to her estate, and if the husband dies it is taken from his estate, as evidence that Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, hired Moses for eight or ten years and made that his bridal gift for his daughter.

We note that the context here says nothing about food, although Moses, peace be upon him, was hungry and had called upon his Lord: ﴿My Lord, indeed I am, for whatever good You send down to me, in need.﴾ [28:24]

However, the people of the histories narrate that Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, offered Moses food and asked him to eat. He said: "I seek Allah's forgiveness," meaning: that I should eat of the food. It was as if this were in exchange for what he had watered for the two girls' flock. For this reason he said: "We are a household that does not sell the work of the Hereafter for all the gold on earth." Shu'ayb said: "Eat, for we are a household that feeds people and hosts guests." He said: "Now I will eat."(1)

(1) Cited by al-Suyuti in ad-Durr al-Manthur (6/407) from Abu Hazim, and attributed by him to Ibn 'Asakir, with similar wording.

Then the Almighty says:
