﴿So when Moses had fulfilled the term and set out with his family, he perceived a fire from the side of the mount. He said to his family, "Wait here, for I have perceived a fire. Perhaps I can bring you news from it, or a burning brand from the fire, that you may warm yourselves."﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when Moses had fulfilled the term...﴾ (al-Qasas), i.e., the term agreed upon with Shu'ayb, peace be upon him. ﴿...and set out with his family...﴾ (al-Qasas). We have said that "ahl" (family) is applied to the wife. In our colloquial language we say "ma'i ahli" (my family) or "al-jama'ah" (the group), meaning the wife. That is because the wife performs for her husband of the interests what a group could not manage, and she surpasses the group with something special that no one else can provide for him, namely the matter of intimate companionship; therefore she takes the place of a group.

The meaning of ﴿perceived...﴾ (al-Qasas) is: he saw, or sensed something of familiarity. ﴿The mount...﴾ (al-Qasas) is the name of the mountain. ﴿He said to his family, "Wait..."﴾ (al-Qasas): wait. ﴿"I have perceived a fire..."﴾ (al-Qasas): he informs her of the existence of the fire, and this means she did not see it as he saw it.

This is evidence that it was not a material fire kindled by a human being; otherwise his family would have shared with him in seeing it. So this, then, was a matter specific to him. ﴿"Perhaps I can bring you news from it..."﴾ (al-Qasas): that is, in hope that I may find someone who will inform us about the road and guide us to where we should head. ﴿"...or a burning brand from the fire, that you may warm yourselves."﴾ (al-Qasas)

﴿He said to his family, "Wait here, for I have perceived a fire. Perhaps I can bring you news from it, or a burning brand from the fire, that you may warm yourselves."﴾ [al-Qasas]

The jadhwah (burning brand): a piece of glowing fire without flame. The meaning of "tasta.lun" is that they warm themselves by it. In another place He said, ﴿with a brand of burning fire...﴾ [an-Naml, 7], meaning a flame with a tongue and blaze. Their purpose in this situation was therefore two things: someone who would show them the way, since their steps had strayed into a place they did not know, and then a brand of fire by which they could warm themselves against the cold.

In another place of this story He did not mention His saying, ﴿Wait...﴾ [al-Qasas]. This is among the points that superficial readers take against the style of the Qur'an. But by reflecting on the situation, we see that it took the form of a dialogue between Moses and his family.

A wife and her husband were enveloped by darkness in a desolate place, where they knew nothing and could not find a path, and the weather was extremely cold. So it is natural that when he tells her, "I have seen a fire; I will go to fetch some of it," she replies, "How can you leave me alone in this place? You may lose your way, or I may lose mine." Then he says to her, ﴿Wait...﴾ [al-Qasas]. Thus this phrase must have been repeated in two forms, as the noble Qur'an recounts.

Likewise, in ﴿I will bring you...﴾ [an-Naml, 7] and in another instance ﴿Perhaps I can bring you...﴾ [al-Qasas, 29]. They said: because he had seen the fire, he said ﴿I will bring you...﴾ [an-Naml, 7] with certainty; but when he reconsidered himself, since it might go out before he reached it, he corrected himself and said ﴿Perhaps I can bring you...﴾ [al-Qasas, 29], as an expression of hope rather than certainty.

1 That is in Surah an-Naml. God Almighty said: ﴿When Moses said to his family, "I have perceived a fire. I will bring you news from it, or bring you a brand of burning fire, that you may warm yourselves."﴾ [an-Naml, 7]

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 28, verse 30:

It is as if the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, wishes to give us a detailed map of the place. Some have said: "from the side of the Mount (al-Tur), and the right side of the Mount." And here: ﴿From the right bank of the valley, in the blessed spot, from the tree...﴾ [al-Qasas 28:30].

The content of the call: ﴿"O Moses, indeed I am Allah, the Lord of the worlds."﴾ [al-Qasas 28:30]. Moses heard this call coming to him from all its directions and flowing in every direction, because Allah, exalted is He, is not confined by a direction. Therefore do not ask: "From where does the voice come?" And he was not accustomed to being addressed by the Lord, blessed and exalted is He.

Along with the call, he sees the fire blazing in a branch of the tree. The fire keeps increasing in blaze, and the tree keeps increasing in greenness. Thus the fire does not burn the tree with its heat, nor does the tree extinguish the fire with its moisture(1). This is, then, an amazing matter in which thought is perplexed. Does he receive all these wonders easily, or must he reflect upon them?

(1) Ibn Abi Hatim related it from Abu Bakr al-Thaqafi, who said: Moses, peace be upon him, came to the tree at night, and it was green while the fire was flickering in it. He went to take hold of the fire, but it veered away from him, so he was struck with alarm and fright. (Cited by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur, 6/413.)

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 28, verse 31:

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says:

﴿And throw down your staff.' But when he saw it moving as though it were a snake, he turned back in retreat and did not return. 'O Moses, come forward and do not fear. Indeed, you are of the secure.'﴾

In another place, his Lord asks him, to put him at ease: ﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Moses?﴾ [Ta-Ha] We have said: Moses, peace be upon him, lengthened this pause in order to prolong the time of intimacy with his Lord. When he sensed that he had gone too far and lengthened it, he said: ﴿And I have in it other uses.﴾ [Ta-Ha] So he expanded at first so that his intimacy with his Lord might increase, then he was brief so that his courtesy toward his Lord would remain.

Here, however, the command comes directly to employ the staff: ﴿And throw down your staff...﴾ [Al-Qasas]

As for His saying: ﴿But when he saw it moving as though it were a snake, he turned back in retreat and did not return...﴾ [Al-Qasas], it is because he saw another marvel, more wondrous than what preceded it. For if we accept the fire blazing in the greenness of the tree, how can we accept that the staff turned into a jann (a jinn-like serpent) that runs and moves?

It would have been possible for the dry staff to turn into a green tree of the same kind as the staff, and that too would be a miracle. But that it should transform into a different kind, passing from the vegetable to the animal, and into an animal that moves and is frightening, this is a strange and unfamiliar thing.

Here there is omitted speech, because the Noble Qur'an is built on brevity. The implied meaning is: So Moses threw down his staff, ﴿and when he saw it moving as though it were a snake, he turned back in retreat...﴾ [Al-Qasas]. This is so that the intellect may be left an opportunity to deduce, and the mind is stirred to follow the events.

As for the jann (serpent): we have said it is the young of the snake, and in this story it has been depicted as jann, thu'ban (large serpent), and hayyah (snake). These are three descriptions of one thing: in its slenderness it is a jann, in its length a thu'ban, and in its thickness a hayyah.

The meaning of ﴿turned back in retreat﴾ [Al-Qasas] is: he departed in fear. ﴿And did not return﴾ [Al-Qasas] means he did not turn around. Then his Lord called to him: ﴿O Moses, come forward and do not fear﴾ [Al-Qasas], meaning: return and do not fear anything. Then He gives him the principle that must accompany him in all his movements in his call: ﴿Indeed, you are of the secure﴾ [Al-Qasas]. He did not say: return, for I will grant you safety in this situation; rather, ﴿indeed, you are of the secure﴾ [Al-Qasas].

That is: this is a continuing principle that clings to you, because you are in the company of Allah, and whoever is in the company of Allah does not fear. Otherwise, if you were afraid now, what would you do before Pharaoh?

Thus the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, gives Moses, peace be upon him, training with Him, and training so that he may confront Pharaoh, his magicians and the whole assembly without fear or trepidation, and so that he may be certain of Allah's victory and support in his final encounter with Pharaoh.

Moses, peace be upon him, benefited from all these situations, and learned from these wonders that he saw, which increased him in confidence and steadfastness. Therefore, when Pharaoh nearly overtook Moses and his people, and they said: ﴿Indeed, we are to be overtaken﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara], Moses, peace be upon him, recalled the principle: ﴿Indeed, you are of the secure﴾ [Al-Qasas], and said with full certainty: ﴿No! Indeed, with me is my Lord; He will guide me﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara].

The confidence that stirred in Moses, peace be upon him, was the company of Allah with him. He said it, and it could seem, at that moment, to be refuted: there was the sea before them and Pharaoh behind them. But it was the confidence of one whom Allah had granted security, and placed in His company and protection.

This security Allah, exalted is He, prescribed for all His prophets and messengers. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And His word has already preceded for Our servants, the messengers. Indeed, they would be the victorious, and indeed, Our soldiers – they would be the predominant﴾ [As-Saffat]

And He said: ﴿O Moses, do not fear. Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence﴾ [An-Naml]

All of this was related to our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), and he benefited from it and trusted in Allah's victory. When his companion, the Siddiq, said to him while they were in the cave: "O Messenger of Allah, if one of them looked down at his feet, he would see us," the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O Abu Bakr, what do you think of two whom Allah is the third of?"(1)

The Qur'an recounts his (ﷺ) saying to his companion: ﴿Do not grieve; indeed, Allah is with us﴾ [At-Tawbah]. As long as we are in the company of the One whom eyes cannot perceive, eyes will not perceive us.

1 Agreed upon. Recorded by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (4663), and likewise by Muslim in his Sahih (2381), from the hadith of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him.

Then the Truth, blessed and exalted, passes Musa (peace be upon him) on to another sign added to his miracles:

﴿Insert your hand into your bosom; it will come out white, without harm. And draw your arm close to your side against fear. These two are proofs from your Lord to Pharaoh and his chiefs. Indeed, they have always been a defiantly disobedient people.﴾ [28:32]

The meaning of ﴿Insert your hand…﴾ [28:32] is: put it into your ﴿bosom﴾ [28:32]. The bosom (jayb) is the opening of a garment at the top, and it was called a jayb because people used to keep their money in the folds of their clothing for safekeeping, so that it would not be stolen. A person would thrust his hand into the neck of his garment until it reached his pocket.

Here we notice the precision of the Qur'anic expression: ﴿it will come out white﴾ [28:32] is not phrased as a command, "and bring it out," as in ﴿Insert your hand﴾ [28:32]. It is as though the process were a mechanism governed with exactness: as soon as he inserts it, it comes out white. His will over his limbs was in the inserting; as for the bringing out, it is by the power of God.

The word ﴿white﴾ [28:32] means radiant, free of disease. Whiteness must be remarkable in Musa (peace be upon him), because he was dark-complexioned; therefore He said ﴿without harm﴾ [28:32], lest they suppose he had some affliction such as leprosy. It is a natural whiteness, yet a miracle.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And draw your arm close to your side against fear﴾ [28:32]: the two wings of a bird are like the two hands of a human. When a person wishes to fly, for example, he does what a bird does when it flies. The meaning is: draw your hands close to you, and fear will leave you.

This process is confirmed by experience: we see a woman, when she sees her child, for example, behaving badly, strike her chest and wail. Our master Ibn ʿAbbas said: whoever is frightened should strike his chest with his hands so that what he encounters of fear departs from him(1). You may try it yourself to learn the truth of this statement.

The meaning of ﴿These two﴾ [28:32]: dhā is a demonstrative for the singular, and we say dhān is a demonstrative for the dual; the kāf is for address. The intended reference is to the two signs, the staff and the hand. ﴿Proofs from your Lord﴾ [28:32], that is, your Lord, the Truth, ﴿to Pharaoh﴾ [28:32], the false lord. Truth and falsehood cannot coexist; falsehood must be annihilated, for it is weak and cannot stand before the might of the Truth: ﴿Rather, We hurl the truth against falsehood, and it crushes it, and behold, it vanishes﴾ [21:18].

Al-burhan (proof): it is the argument and evidence for the truth of what is being proven. ﴿To Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾ [28:32], because Pharaoh claimed divinity, and his chiefs made fools of their people, who obeyed him. ﴿Indeed, they have always been a defiantly disobedient people﴾ [28:32], that is, Pharaoh and the chiefs all together. ﴿Defiantly disobedient﴾ [28:32], that is, those who have come out of obedience, from our saying "fasaqat al-ruṭba," meaning it came out of its skin.

What is meant here is the religious veil that envelops a person, protects him, and keeps him from being affected by the factors of sin. When he strips off this garment, removes this veil, and rebels against the method, his nakedness is exposed and his shame becomes evident.

(1) Cited by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir (7/5170), who said: "Ibn ʿAbbas said: No one who is overcome by terror after Musa (peace be upon him) puts his hand on his chest and then the terror leaves him."
Musa (peace be upon him) was still fearful about the matter of having killed the Egyptian man; therefore he asks his Lord to support him and to help him with his brother.

The meaning of ridʾ (ردء) is helper, one who supports.

We know from the story of Moses, peace be upon him, while he was a child in the house of Pharaoh, that a speech impediment afflicted his tongue, so his speech was heavy and his tongue did not speak clearly. Therefore he wished to seek the eloquence of his brother Aaron to support him, to make his argument manifest, and to remove doubts from him.

Moses could have asked his Lord to make his brother Aaron a helper, so that Aaron would be a part of Moses' own self. But he loved for his brother to share in his mission and to attain this virtue and this elevated rank. So he said: ﴿So send him with me as a helper, to confirm me.﴾ That is, one who supports me, so that people do not deny me, and so that he becomes a messenger like me by commission from God.

Therefore we see the verses speak of Aaron as a messenger who is a partner to Moses in his mission. Concerning both of them, He, exalted is He, says: ﴿Go, you and your brother, to Pharaoh; indeed, he has transgressed. And speak to him with gentle speech that perhaps he may remember or fear.﴾ [Ta-Ha]

If we look at the unity of the message, they are one messenger, and this is clear in His saying: ﴿So come to Pharaoh and say: "Indeed, we are messengers of the Lord of the worlds."﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara']

And it came in Pharaoh's saying: ﴿Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is mad.﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara'] in the singular form. It is like when the president of a republic sends a message with two or three people to his counterpart in another state; we call all of them collectively "messenger," because their message is one. So if you look at the unity of the message from the sender to the one to whom it is sent, they are one; and if you look at each individually, they are two messengers.

It has also come: ﴿Indeed, we are two messengers of your Lord...﴾ [Ta-Ha], so He addressed them once in the singular and once in the dual.

Therefore, when Moses, peace be upon him, invoked against the people of Pharaoh, when wealth deceived them and the adornment of the worldly life tempted them, he said: ﴿Our Lord, obliterate their wealth and harden their hearts, so they will not believe until they see the painful punishment.﴾ [Yunus]

The speaker here is Moses alone, yet He, exalted is He, said: ﴿He said, "Your supplication has been answered, so remain on a straight path."﴾ [Yunus] So He regarded them as one messenger: Moses supplicates and Aaron says "Amin" to his supplication, and the one who says Amin is one of the two who supplicate.

(1) From ʿIkrimah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: Moses, peace be upon him, would supplicate and Aaron, peace be upon him, would say Amin. This is His saying: ﴿He said, "Your supplication has been answered"﴾ [Yunus]. Cited by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur (4/385), attributed to ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 28, verse 35:

He answered him, his Lord: ﴿We will strengthen your arm through your brother.﴾ [al-Qasas] This is because Moses said in another place: ﴿Strengthen my back through him, and make him a partner in my task.﴾ [Ta-Ha 31-32]. And His saying, exalted is He, ﴿We will strengthen your arm through your brother﴾ [al-Qasas 35] is an eloquent expression that fits what was asked of Moses, because a person carries out most or nearly all of his works with his hands, and the muscle that performs lifting and movement is the arm (ʿadd).

Therefore, when we praise a person for strength, we say: "So-and-so is muscular (ʿadil)." And when a person, God forbid, is afflicted with muscle atrophy, you find him frail, unable to do anything. So the meaning is: We will strengthen you with physical strength.

﴿And We will give you both authority﴾ [al-Qasas 35] This is the moral strength, which is the strength of argument, logic and proof. So He combined for them two kinds of strength: physical strength and moral strength.

Therefore He said after it: ﴿so they shall not reach you﴾ [al-Qasas 35], meaning: We will save you from them. But the struggle between truth and falsehood does not end with the salvation of the people of truth; rather, it is necessary that they be victorious over the people of falsehood. There is a difference between a man whose enemy attacks him so he closes the door in front of him, and the matter ends at this point, and one who confronts his enemy and contends with him until he defeats him, thereby preventing harm to himself and inflicting harm upon his enemy.

This is what is meant by His saying, exalted is He, ﴿You two and those who follow you will be the victors﴾ [al-Qasas 35]. Thus God removed from them the passivity of harm and granted them the positivity of victory.

We note the placement of the phrase ﴿by Our signs﴾ [al-Qasas 35] between the two expressions: ﴿so they shall not reach you﴾ [al-Qasas 35] and ﴿You two and those who follow you will be the victors﴾ [al-Qasas 35]. It is thus a cause for both: by Our signs and Our manifest miracles We will save you, and by Our signs and Our miracles We will give you victory. It is one word serving both meanings, and this is among the aspects of the eloquence of the Noble Qur'an.

Among the wonders of the Qur'an's vocabulary is the word (al-najm) in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The sun and the moon [move] by calculation, and the stars [an-najm] and the trees prostrate.﴾ [al-Rahman 5-6]. Here "an-najm" comes between the sun and the moon, which are two heavenly signs, and the tree, which is a plant of the earth. Therefore "an-najm" is apt in the sense of a star of the sky, or in the sense of a small plant without a stem, like the grass that livestock graze in the desert.[2]

Therefore the poet said:
"I watch the stars (an-najm) on my journey to you, and my steed grazes on the desert herbage."

1 Al-azr: strength. And "azarahu": he strengthened him. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/18].
2 Abu Ishaq said: It has been said that an-najm is meant to refer to the stars (plural), and he said: It is permissible that an-najm here be what grows on the surface of the earth and what rises of the stars of the sky. And it is said of everything that rises: "qad najama" (it has risen).

Then the Truthful One, glory be to Him, says:

﴿So when Moses came to them with Our clear signs, they said, "This is nothing but fabricated magic, and we have not heard of this among our first forefathers."﴾

His words, exalted is He, ﴿with Our clear signs﴾ [al-Qasas]: that is, with Our miracles, manifest and dazzling. So when they were stunned before the signs of Allah and bewildered as to how to get out of this predicament—Moses had come to demolish the throne of false divinity held by Pharaoh—they had no recourse but to say: ﴿This is nothing but fabricated magic, and we have not heard of this among our first forefathers.﴾

Therefore, the Truthful One—blessed and exalted is He—teaches Moses, peace be upon him, how to argue with these people. It is as if He said to him: "You are going to face people who cling to falsehood, who are greedy for it, and who profit from it. They will certainly become angry if you overturn their falsehood and turn them away from it toward the truth. They have grown accustomed to falsehood, so if you bring them out of what they are accustomed to into what they are not accustomed to, you must be gentle and must not provoke them, lest you combine the harshness of abandoning what they had become used to with the harshness of calling them to what they are not used to."

It is enough that you will strip them of the authority of divinity under whose shadow they have lived. If you increase the harshness against them, you will produce in them obstinacy and stubbornness in dispute.

Therefore the Exalted said: ﴿Speak to him with gentle words﴾ [Ta-Ha 44]—meaning: excuse him for what he meets with when his divinity is taken from him and he becomes one of the subjects.

And if they confront you with harshness, as they said: ﴿This is nothing but fabricated magic, and we have not heard of this among our first forefathers﴾ [al-Qasas 36], then you confront them with gentleness.

Consider here the gentleness and the courtesy of disputation displayed by Musa (peace be upon him). He did not answer them with the harshness he had heard from them, nor did he accuse them as they had accused him. Rather, he responded in this tactful manner and with this allusive hint: ﴿My Lord knows best who has come with guidance from Him, and whose will be the good outcome of the abode.﴾ [al-Qasas 28:37] He did not say: "I have come with guidance."

Then he said: ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed.﴾ [al-Qasas 28:37], whether it is we or you, and he did not say "you are the wrongdoers." He stated the matter in general terms and left it to minds to discern.

The meaning of ﴿the abode﴾ [al-Qasas 28:37] is: the world (al-dunya). And its outcome ('aqibah) means: the Hereafter (al-akhirah).

We have seen this prophetic courtesy in disputation and dialogue in the biography of our master, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), with the disbelievers of Makkah and his obstinate opponents, and his Lord addressed him: ﴿And do not argue with the People of the Scripture except in a manner that is best.﴾ [al-'Ankabut 29:46]

The reason is that you will be bringing them out of the falsehood they have loved and become accustomed to, into the truth which they dislike, so do not combine two harshnesses upon them. Therefore, at the height of the disbelievers' harm to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he would say: ((O Allah, guide my people, for they do not know)).(1)

May Allah have mercy on Shawqi, who expressed this matter in a concise phrase, saying: "Advice is heavy, so do not send it as a mountain, nor make it a dispute." Your advice means that you are saying to the one before you: "You are in error and I am in the right." So, for him to listen to you, you must first win him over to yourself so that he accepts from you, and you must not wound his feelings, lest he increase in obstinacy and arrogance. How similar the one in error is to the sick person who needs someone to take him by the hand and soothe (2) his illness.

They have illustrated this with a person who is drowning, while his companion on the shore blames him for entering the sea, though he does not know how to swim. So he said to him: ("Rescue me, then advise me") — save me first and reach me, then say whatever you wish.

Another said: "Truths are bitter, so lend them the lightness of expression."

As for when the adviser despairs of the response of the one advised, as in the story of the Prophet of Allah Nuh (peace be upon him), who continued calling his people for a thousand years less fifty years, then the matter differs. The Prophet was patient with his people, hoping that they would return to their right guidance, or that they might produce righteous offspring who would accept what their fathers rejected.

How long was Nuh's patience with his people, and how great was his courtesy in dialogue with them, when, having been accused of lying and fabrication, he said to them: ﴿If I have invented it, then upon me is my crime, and I am free of what you commit.﴾ [Hud 11:35]

He attributed the crime to himself so as to place himself on level with them, hoping to win their hearts. But, since it was within Allah's knowledge that they would never believe, and there was no benefit from them or from their successive generations, and after Nuh had spent this long life in calling them, Allah commanded him to invoke against them, since there was no hope of their guidance. So he said: ﴿My Lord, do not leave upon the earth from among the disbelievers a single dweller (dayyar).(3) Indeed, if You leave them, they will mislead Your servants and will beget none but wicked, disbelieving offspring.﴾ [Nuh 71:26-27]

And Muhammad (ﷺ), in his dialogue with the disbelievers of Makkah, says: ﴿You will not be asked about what we have committed, and we will not be asked about what you do.﴾ [Saba' 34:25]

Glory be to Allah, what humility is this, and what abundant courtesy in winning people over! He attributes the crime to himself though he is the Messenger of Allah, and when he speaks about them he says ﴿you do⁠﴾ [Saba' 34:25], calling their crime, their harm, and their disbelief "deed." Had he said as his brother Nuh said, it would have been humility on his part (peace and blessings be upon him).

(1) Al-Suyuti cited it in al-Durr al-Manthur (3/117) at his saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah will protect you from the people﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:67], and attributed it to Ibn 'Abbas (narrated by Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah). He also cited it (3/481) from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud: "I saw the Prophet (ﷺ) wiping blood from his face while he related about one of the prophets, and he was saying: 'O Allah, guide my people, for they do not know.'" Narrated by Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad in al-Zuhd, Abu Nu'aym and Ibn 'Asakir.

(2) Al-Asa: treatment and remedy. And al-Isa': the very medicine. [Lisan al-'Arab, root: asa]

(3) Dayyar: anyone. It is said: "There is not a dayyar in the house," meaning: there is no one in it. [Lisan al-'Arab, root: dayr]

Then Allah, glorified is He, says:

{And Pharaoh said, "O chiefs, I know of no god for you other than myself. So kindle for me, O Haman, [a fire] upon the clay and make for me a lofty tower, that I may look upon the god of Moses, though indeed I think he is among the liars."}

Pharaoh feared the effect of Moses' words upon his people, and imagined that they would be affected by them as we say ("brainwashing"). So he wanted to remind them of his divinity, and that he had not been moved by what he heard from Moses: ﴿O chiefs, I know of no god for you other than myself﴾ [al-Qasas 28:38]. That is to say: beware of believing Moses' words, for I am your god, and you have no god other than me.

Then he confirms this divinity, saying to Haman, his minister: ﴿So kindle for me, O Haman, [a fire] upon the clay and make for me a lofty tower, that I may look upon the god of Moses﴾ [al-Qasas 28:38]. In another place he said: ﴿O Haman, build for me a tower that I may reach the means, the means of the heavens, and look upon the god of Moses﴾ [Ghafir 40:36-37].

It is as if he wanted to satisfy his people. Here he wants to search for the god whom Moses claims, as though if he built a tower and ascended it, he would see the Lord of Moses. But did Haman build this tower for him? He built nothing for him, which indicates that the matter was pure jest upon jest, and a mockery of the people whom he made light of and toyed with their minds.

And otherwise, what need did they have to fire the clay to make these red bricks that we see and build with now, while they had the stones and granite with which they built the pyramids and carved statues from them? The process of firing clay requires much time and effort. So the matter is: gaining time from the adversary, and stupefying his chiefs.

As for his saying ﴿that I may look upon the god of Moses﴾ [al-Qasas 28:38], before he reaches a judgment on whether he sees the god of Moses or does not see him, he hastens to pass judgment on Moses: ﴿and indeed I think he is among the liars﴾ [al-Qasas 28:38]; in order to divert his chiefs from the words of Moses.

Note 1: al-Sarh (صرح): a lofty palace. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/373]. Ibn Manzur said in [Lisan al-Arab – root: ṣ-r-ḥ]: "al-Sarh is a single building built apart, massive and tall toward the sky; it is said: it is every lofty, elevated building."

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 28, verse 39:

Meaning: they were arrogant without any right, and without any justification for arrogance. They had none of these justifications, because a person is arrogant when his greatness is inherent in himself. As for greatness that is bestowed upon you by others, you do not become arrogant through it. Whoever is arrogant is arrogant through something inherent in him, as they say: "The one who sews, sews on his hip" (i.e., one works with the tools of his own trade; a proverb meaning that everyone works from what is his own).

The same applies to the other causes of arrogance: wealth, strength, rank, authority, and so on.

Therefore God Most High dislikes the arrogant, and He says in the Hadith Qudsi:

("Pride is My garment, and greatness is My cloak; whoever disputes with Me over either of them, I will cast him into Hell.")(1)

Pride and greatness are attributes of majesty and beauty belonging to God Most High, which make everyone equal before the pride of God, so no one is arrogant toward another ("and we all tend to be equal in our faults"). Under the shade of God's pride, which protects our humility, if one of us were arrogant toward another, he would be arrogant through something granted to him, not inherent in himself. Therefore God gives victory to the one over whom you are arrogant, and makes him higher than you. In our rural areas they say: "Whoever throws his brother's fault at him will not die until he sees it in himself."

The arrogant person, in reality, is deficient in faith, because he is only arrogant when he sees all people beneath him. Had he kept in mind the pride of his Creator, he would have been ashamed to be arrogant in His presence. Thus was the arrogance of Pharaoh and his soldiers in the land, without right.

As for arrogance undertaken to protect the weak so that they may live in its shade, that is arrogance in truth. Therefore, when the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, describes Himself as "the Great, the Arrogant," we say: this is true, because it is a protection for all of us from some of us being arrogant toward others.

As for His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And they thought that they would not be returned to Us﴾ [al-Qasas 39]: their arrogance in the land came as a result of their thinking that they would not return to God, and that He had created and provided for them, then they slipped away from Him and would never return to Him. But far from it; as you say, there must be a return for them.

(1) Narrated by Ahmad in his Musnad (2/376, 414), Ibn Majah in his Sunan (4174), and Abu Dawud in his Sunan (4090), from the hadith of Abu Hurairah, may Allah be pleased with him.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 28, verse 40:

It is as if the Truth, glorified is He, did not give them respite until they returned to Him on the Day of Resurrection; rather, He hastened their punishment in this world before the punishment of the Hereafter. ﴿So We seized him and his soldiers⦁﴾ That is: all of them, in one grasp, the follower and the followed. ﴿So We cast them into the sea⦁﴾ We threw them into the sea. This seizing, which encompasses all of them in one grasp, indicates the power of the One who seizes, and this is a matter that none can accomplish except Allah, the Strong, the Mighty.

As He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And thus is the seizing of your Lord when He seizes the cities while they are wrongdoing. Indeed, His seizure is painful and severe.﴾ [Hud: 102]

The seizing of a human being is not described as having strength except in His, exalted is He, saying, urging us to take the paths of goodness with strength: ﴿Take what We have given you with strength⦁﴾ [al-Baqarah: 93]

Then He, glorified is He, says: ﴿So look, how was the end of the wrongdoers?⦁﴾ [al-Qasas: 40] That is: their final outcome. It was a marvel among the marvels of time and a sign among the signs of Allah. The sea and the water are among the soldiers of Allah: they support the truth and defeat falsehood. We have already mentioned how Allah saved Musa, peace be upon him, and destroyed Fir'awn by one and the same thing, when Allah commanded Musa to strike the sea with his staff, so every part of it became like a great mountain.

When Musa and his people had crossed to the other side, he wanted to strike the sea again, so that the water would return to its flowing and passage; Allah corrected him and commanded him to leave it in its state. The Truth, blessed and exalted is He, follows His Prophet Musa step by step, as He said to him: ﴿Indeed, I am with you both, hearing and seeing⦁﴾ [Ta-Ha: 46]

Far be it from Allah that He would assign him a matter and then abandon him. When Fir'awn saw the dry path before him, he crossed with his soldiers, and Allah closed the sea over them, so they became a sign and a lesson, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿So today We will save you in your body, that you may be a sign for those who come after you⦁﴾ [Yunus: 92]

And reflect on the power of Allah that saved Musa from drowning, when his mother had cast him into the water with her own hands, and drowned Fir'awn.

¹ Likewise in His saying: ﴿O Yahya, take the Book with strength⦁﴾ [Maryam: 12]. The author of Zilal al-Qur'an (4/2304) says: "Yahya inherited from his father Zakariyya, and he was called upon to bear the burden and to rise with the trust in strength and resolve, not weakening, not slackening, and not retreating from the duties of the inheritance."

Imams: plural of imam, meaning one who is followed. The follower is subordinate to his imam. So if we were in prayer, we would not bow until he bows, nor rise until he rises; our following of him is obligatory. If he errs, the follower must alert him and remind him, saying to him: "Subhan Allah (Glory be to God), be alert to a mistake on your part." Thus we are followers of him only in what is right; if he errs, we deviate from him.

The imam is an example and a model for the followers in goodness and the path of truth, as the Exalted said concerning His Prophet Ibrahim (peace be upon him):
﴿And when Ibrahim was tried by his Lord with words, and he fulfilled them, He said: "Indeed, I will make you an imam (leader) for the people." ...124﴾ [al-Baqarah]

Then Ibrahim (peace be upon him) wished that the imamate would remain in his offspring after him, so he said: ﴿And of my descendants?...124﴾ [al-Baqarah]. God corrected him and informed him that the imamate is not attained except by people of goodness: ﴿He said: "My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers."124﴾ [al-Baqarah]

Likewise, when Nuh (peace be upon him) called upon his Lord: ﴿My Lord, indeed my son is of my family...45﴾ [Hud], God corrected him: ﴿Indeed, he is not of your family; indeed, he is one whose deeds are not righteous...46﴾ [Hud]

So: eligibility for prophethood and eligibility for imamate are matters of action and conduct, not of kinship or lineage.

Imamate may also be in evil, like that of which we are speaking: ﴿And We made them imams calling to the Fire...41﴾ [al-Qasas]. They are a bad example and a model of evil. The noble hadith has come: "Whoever establishes a good practice in Islam will have its reward and the reward of whoever acts by it until the Day of Resurrection, and whoever establishes an evil practice will bear its burden and the burden of whoever acts by it until the Day of Resurrection."¹

The Exalted says concerning the leaders of evil example: ﴿That they may bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection, and of the burdens of those whom they mislead without knowledge...25﴾ [al-Nahl]

Pharaoh and his chiefs were thus an example in evil, and an example in misguidance, terror and tyranny; and likewise they will be imams and leaders in the Hereafter, but toward the Fire: ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection they will not be helped...41﴾ [al-Qasas]

¹ Narrated by Ahmad in his Musnad (4/361) and Ibn Majah in his Sunan (203), from the hadith of Jarir ibn Abd Allah (may Allah be pleased with him).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 28, verse 42:

The Almighty's saying: ﴿And We made them follow up with a curse in this world⦆ [al-Qasas 42] means: We made a curse follow them. So whoever mentions them in this world says, "May Allah curse them." Upon them is a lasting curse that remains as long as the world remains. This cursing and expulsion from Allah's mercy is not the recompense for their deeds; rather it is a prelude to a punishment that remains and is eternal in the Hereafter, as the Almighty said: ﴿And indeed, for those who have done wrong is a punishment besides that⦆ [al-Tur 47].

﴿And on the Day of Resurrection they will be among the reviled⦆ [al-Qasas 42]. The root is q-b-h (qabaha). You say to the wicked, "May Allah disfigure you (qabahaka Allah)," meaning: may He expel you and distance you from good. It has another usage: you say, "I qabahta the boil (qabahtu al-damal)," meaning: I opened it and lanced it before it ripened, so that blood comes out along with pus, and its place becomes disfigured.

We have said before: if you leave a boil to the divine pharmacy in your body until it heals by the body's immunity and its resistance, you find that it leaves no trace; but if you intervene with medicines and surgery, it must leave a trace and disfigure the place.

The meaning, then, is: ﴿they are among the reviled⦆ [al-Qasas 42], i.e., those whose faces have been disfigured after the smoothness and freshness of their skin. The Qur'an has expressed this disfigurement in various images.

The Almighty says: ﴿Faces on that day will have upon them dust, covered by darkness⦆ [Abasa 40-41].

He, glorified is He, says: ﴿On the Day when some faces will turn white and some faces will turn black⦆ [Al 'Imran 106].

And He says: ﴿And We will gather the criminals that Day blue-eyed⦆ [Ta-Ha 102].

It is known that the bluishness of the body comes only as a result of severe blows and bruises that cause harmful reactions under the skin, so that it turns blue; likewise the blueness of the eye. Among eye diseases is glaucoma (al-mayah al-zarqa'), which is more dangerous than the white kind.

Therefore the poet says:
"For the miser, over his wealth, are faults: blue eyes, and upon them black faces."
Because he is greedy for his wealth and does not want to spend it.

Blue is used for ugliness and intimidation. In the Middle Ages they would paint the faces of soldiers blue to frighten and terrify enemies, and people came to know it as the color of the devil. Therefore in our colloquial language we say "the blue ghouls" (al-'afarit al-zurq), and in dispraise we say "so-and-so has a blue fang" (fulan nabuhu azraq).

The poet says:
"Will he kill me while the Musharrafi swords are upon my bed, and sharpened blue ones like the fangs of ghouls?"

As for black, it is meant to denote a disfigured, repulsive face; otherwise black is not dispraised in itself as a color. We often see a person of dark complexion radiating attractiveness and cheerfulness, such that one does not tire of looking at him, and it is known that beauty has no color.

Allah, the Exalted, bestows beauty and cheerfulness and makes them radiate in all forms. You may see in some faces of black color a glow and radiance, and you may see a person of white color looking drawn and gloomy, without vitality.

1 The poet is Imru' al-Qays.
2 The Musharrafi swords are attributed to villages in the land of Yemen; it is said they are from the land of the Arabs near the countryside. [Lisan al-'Arab, root: sh-r-f]
3 al-Jahiz said in his book (al-Hayawan) (6/158), edited by 'Abd al-Salam Harun: "al-Aghwal: the name for every jinn-thing that appears to travellers and changes into various forms and garments, whether male or female, though most of their speech is that it is female." The verse is in the Diwan of Imru' al-Qays, 33; al-Kamil of al-Mubarrad (2/79); and Husn al-Tawassul ila Sina'at al-Tarassul of Shihab al-Din Mahmud al-Halabi, p. 112.

Then the Truthful, glory be to Him, says: {And We certainly gave Moses the Book after We had destroyed the earlier generations, as insight for mankind, and guidance and mercy, that they might remember} (28:43).

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book after We had destroyed the earlier generations...﴾ (28:43), namely the people of Noah, ʿĀd, Thamūd and others. The meaning is that Moses, peace be upon him, came as a barrier and intermediary between messengers whose nations denied them, so Allah seized them with punishment. The messengers before Moses did not fight; rather, the messenger from among them would convey the message and manifest the proof, and they would demand signs. If Allah answered them and they denied, Allah would bring the punishment upon them.

As the Glorified said:

﴿So each We seized for his sin. Among them were those upon whom We sent a storm of pebbles, and among them were those who were seized by the blast, and among them were those whom We caused the earth to swallow, and among them were those whom We drowned. And Allah would not wrong them, but they were wronging themselves.﴾ (29:40)

All of this is the punishment of total annihilation, leaving not a single one of the deniers.

Then Moses, peace be upon him, came as a barrier between the punishment of annihilation from Allah, Exalted, upon the deniers without intervention of the messengers in the matter of punishment, and the message of Muhammad (ﷺ), for Allah commanded him to fight the disbelievers and deniers without bringing down upon them the punishment of annihilation. That is because his message is general in time and place until the Hour is established, and he (ﷺ) is entrusted with the lives of all creation.

Therefore the Exalted says concerning the matter of fighting in the era of Moses, peace be upon him: ﴿Have you not considered the chiefs of the Children of Israel after Moses...﴾ (2:246), i.e., in his time and age: ﴿when they said to a prophet of theirs, "Appoint for us a king, and we will fight in the way of Allah." He said, "Would you perhaps refrain from fighting if fighting is prescribed for you?" They said, "And what is [wrong] with us that we should not fight in the way of Allah while we have been expelled from our homes and our children?" But when fighting was prescribed for them, they turned away, except for a few of them...﴾ (2:246)

It has been reported that our master, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), said: "Allah did not punish any people, nor any generation, nor any nation, nor the people of any town, since Allah sent down the Torah to Moses."

It is as if the punishment of annihilation ended with the descent of the Torah, and an exception was made of only one town, which is (Aylah), located between Madyan and Jordan.

And the Truthful, blessed and exalted, gives us the first experience of a mission, and the intervention of the messengers in the story of Moses, peace be upon him.

It is narrated from Abu Umamah that he said: "I was under the saddle of the Messenger of Allah" — meaning, holding the saddle of the Messenger's she-camel — "on the day of the Conquest, and I heard him say fine and beautiful words, and among what he said was: 'Any man of the People of the Book who believes in me has two rewards — that is, the reward of his belief in Moses or in Jesus, and the reward of his belief in me — he has what we have and he bears what we bear.'"

This means that fighting had not yet been prescribed for them.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book...﴾ (28:43), i.e., the Torah; ﴿after We had destroyed the earlier generations...﴾ (28:43), i.e., without intervention of prophets; ﴿as insight for mankind...﴾ (28:43), i.e., We gave him the Book to be a light guiding them, an insight leading them aright, and illuminating their hearts; ﴿and guidance and mercy...﴾ (28:43), guidance to the path of good, and mercy that protects the society from the corruption of false methods and protects them from being among the people of the Fire; ﴿that they might remember﴾ (28:43).

Remembrance means that you had a matter, then you forgot it, so you need someone to remind you of it; it is not new to you. This matter is the innate nature (fitrah):

﴿The nature of Allah upon which He created mankind...﴾ (30:30)

But this sound nature is beset by the desires and appetites of the soul, and heedlessness and forgetfulness come upon it. Therefore the Truthful, glory be to Him, reminds people of what they had neglected of the way of truth. So, within the sound nature placed in every soul are the foundations of faith and guidance, were it not for human heedlessness.

1 Here Allah mentions four types of punishment:
- ﴿Among them were those upon whom We sent a storm of pebbles﴾ (29:40): they are the people of ʿĀd. Allah sent upon them a violent wind that carried the pebbles of the earth, cast them down upon them, and uprooted them from the ground.
- ﴿and among them were those who were seized by the blast﴾ (29:40): they are the people of Thamūd; a blast came upon them that silenced their voices and movements.
- ﴿and among them were those whom We caused the earth to swallow﴾ (29:40): it is Qārūn; Allah caused the earth to swallow him and his dwelling, and he will keep sinking into it until the Day of Resurrection.
- ﴿and among them were those whom We drowned﴾ (29:40): it is Pharaoh and his minister Hāmān and their armies, every one of them. [Tafsīr Ibn Kathīr 3/413]
2 Reported by al-Ḥākim in his Mustadrak (4/408) from the hadith of Abu Saʿīd al-Khudrī with the wording: "Allah did not destroy any people, nor any generation, nor any nation, nor the people of any town, since He sent down the Torah upon the face of the earth, with a punishment from the sky, except the people of the town that were transformed into apes." He said: sound according to the conditions of the two Shaykhs, though they did not record it. Al-Haythamī said in Majmaʿ al-Zawāʾid (7/88): "Al-Bazzār narrated it both as a mawqūf and as a marfūʿ report, and its narrators are the narrators of the Sahih."
3 Reported by Ibn Majah in his Sunan (1956) and Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr in his Sunan (913) from the hadith of Abu Mūsā al-Ashʿarī, and its wording is: "Three will be given their reward twice: a man of the People of the Book who believed in his prophet and then met the Prophet (ﷺ), believed in him, and followed him — he has two rewards."

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 28, verse 44:

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says:

{And you were not on the western side when We decreed to Moses the command, nor were you among the witnesses.}

His saying: ﴿on the western side...﴾ [al-Qasas: 44] means: the western side of the blessed place, at the tree, and it is the place where God spoke to Moses and sent him. ﴿When We decreed to Moses the command...﴾ [al-Qasas: 44] means: We commanded him with a command that was definitively decided, and it was the Message.

﴿Nor were you among the witnesses﴾ [al-Qasas: 44].

You may ask: if the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was not a witness to these events, then who informed him of them? We say: God, exalted is He, informed him. If you say: perhaps another person informed him of them, or he read them in the books of earlier peoples.

We say: his people testified concerning him that he was unlettered (ummi), who neither reads nor writes, and it was not known of him that he sat on any day with a teacher. Likewise they knew his conduct in his life, his journeys and his travels, and there was nothing in them of these events.

Therefore, when they accused the Messenger of God that he had sat with a teacher, and said, as the Qur'an relates: ﴿And We certainly know that they say, "It is only a human who teaches him."﴾ [al-Nahl: 103]

The Qur'an answered them plainly: ﴿The tongue of the one they refer to is foreign, while this is a clear Arabic tongue.﴾ [al-Nahl: 103]

They meant by that two Roman blacksmiths (rumiyyan haddadayn) whom the Messenger of God frequented. And likewise the nation to which the Messenger of God was sent was an unlettered nation (ummiyya), so from whom then did he learn?

If being unlettered (al-ummiyya) is a blameworthy attribute from which we recoil, so that one of the superficial-minded says: "Do not call the Messenger of God unlettered," we say: if unlettered-ness is a blemish, it is a distinction with respect to the Messenger of God (ﷺ); because the ummi means one attributed to the mother (umm), and remains in his natural state, knowing nothing.

Read His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And God brought you out of the wombs of your mothers, knowing nothing.﴾ [al-Nahl: 78] And we say in proverb: "So-and-so is just as his mother bore him," meaning he knows nothing, and this is a blemish in ordinary human beings, because he has not attached himself to those around him and has not benefited from the experiences of life.

As for unlettered-ness with the Messenger of God, it is an honour; because the highest attainment of a learner in any nation is that he takes a portion of knowledge from his fellow humans, so he becomes indebted to them for this knowledge. But the Messenger of God learned from the Highest Knowing One, so no one influenced his knowledge, and no one has any favour or obligation upon him.

Therefore the whole world marvels at the Arab nation, this unlettered, nomadic nation not bound by any law, rather each tribe among them has its own law. They marvel: how did this nation come to lead the world, and how did its civilization conquer the world within half a century?

If the Arabs were a civilized nation, they would have called Islam a civilizational leap, as they said after our victory in October, when our men saw extraordinary things fighting alongside them, so much so that they did not doubt that it was support from God, exalted is He, for an army that began the battle with the cry "God is greatest." But on the third day of the battle there emerged in our newspapers someone who said: "It is a civilizational victory," and on the same day the breach was opened at (the Deversoir).

Strange is the matter of these people from our own kin: why do you reject God's grace and deny His support for you? And what troubles you about a victory that came with reinforcement from God? Have you not read: ﴿And none knows the hosts of your Lord except Him﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31]? And after the breach was opened, what did you offer to close it? Come with your civilizational thinking and extract us from this predicament.

And if you find it hard to admit God's soldiers among their ranks, is not the engineer who was guided to the idea of using water pressure to open the path at (Bar-Lev) through which the soldiers could pass, is he not among God's soldiers?

This idea had cost us much time and effort without benefit, until there came this man whom God illuminated in insight and guided to this operation, which did not come about by chance, but was the result of faith in God, nearness to Him, and supplication to Him. So may God reward him on behalf of Egypt and Islam with good.

And it is strange that, after the end of the war, they conducted a theatrical rehearsal of the war, when they had been unable to cross the Bar-Lev line while in a state of security and peace.

Returning to the question of illiteracy: we say to those who call for eradicating illiteracy among people, that they should teach them from human knowledge: would that you had said, "Let us eradicate illiteracy among them so that we may teach them about God."

So His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you were not on the western side when We decreed to Moses the command, nor were you among the witnesses﴾ [al-Qasas: 44] means: Muhammad did not see these events nor was present at them. And from the same usage is His saying about the month of Ramadan: ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185], meaning: is present in it.

1 "Alhada ila al-shay'": he pointed to it. Its meaning: the tongue of the one they point to is foreign, because they used to say: the Messenger is taught by a foreign man. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/189].
2 'Ubaydullah ibn Muslim said: We had two Roman slaves who would read a book of theirs in their own language, and the Prophet (ﷺ) would pass by them, stop and listen to them. The polytheists said: he learns from them, so God revealed this verse. Reported by Ibn Kathir in his tafsir (2/587).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 28, verse 46:

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿And you were not on the side of the mount when We called [Moses]﴾ [Al-Qasas]: that is, Moses, peace be upon him. ﴿But it is a mercy from your Lord﴾ [Al-Qasas]: that is, you, O Muhammad, did not witness these events; rather, they came to you as a decisive revelation from Allah, ﴿that you may warn a people to whom no warner had come before you, that they may remember﴾ [Al-Qasas]: they may remember what they had neglected of the sound natural disposition (fitrah) upon which Allah created mankind.

The phrase "and you were not" (wa ma kunta) in several places in the Qur'an indicates that the Messenger of Allah brought reports which he had not read in any book, nor had he heard them from a teacher, since he could not read, and it is not known of him that he sat with any teacher. The People of the Book are the ones who recognise the truth of these reports, because they are mentioned in their books; therefore the Qur'an says of them: ﴿They recognise him as they recognise their own sons﴾ [Al-An'am: 20].

And He, glorified is He, says: ﴿Indeed, this is in the former scriptures, the scriptures of Abraham and Moses﴾ [Al-A'la: 18-19].

Among the signs of prophethood is that Allah, the Truthful, tears away for His Prophet, peace be upon him, the veils of the unseen (hujub al-ghayb). A thing may be hidden from you either because it is past and you have no means of reaching it; this is the veil of the past time, which is known only through reading a book or learning from a teacher, and Allah has negated this in respect of the Messenger, peace be upon him. Or the veil may be that of the future time and of events that have not yet come, which none can tell you of except the One who knows them from eternity.

Therefore the Exalted says to His Prophet, peace be upon him: ﴿We shall make you recite, and you will not forget﴾ [Al-A'la: 6]. So the Qur'an would descend upon the Messenger of Allah in portions, and when the revelation had passed from him he would dictate it to his companions, each verse in its place and order within the surah (1), and then he would recite it afterwards exactly as it had been revealed and as he had dictated it.

We have previously said: you can challenge any person to speak, for example, for a third of an hour and then repeat what he said, and he will not be able to do so. But the matter with our master the Messenger of Allah is different, because it is from Allah, the Exalted: ﴿We shall make you recite, and you will not forget﴾ [Al-A'la: 6].

We have also said: at the beginning of the descent of the Qur'an upon our master the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, he would repeat the verse after Jibril, peace be upon him, for fear of forgetting it. If Jibril said: ﴿By the morning brightness﴾ [Ad-Duha: 1], the Messenger of Allah would say: ﴿By the morning brightness﴾ [Ad-Duha: 1], and so on. So Allah revealed to him: ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it. Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recital. So when We have recited it, follow its recital﴾ [Al-Qiyamah: 16-18].

And He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And do not rush with the Qur'an before its revelation to you has been completed﴾ [Ta-Ha: 114].

That is: relieve yourself, O Muhammad, and do not fear forgetting; wait until the verses are finished, and you will repeat them as they are, not forgetting from them a single letter.

Among the unveilings of the veil of the future is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And horses, mules and donkeys for you to ride and as adornment﴾ [An-Nahl: 8]. Had the verse ended at this point, they would have said: the Qur'an mentions only the primitive things and says nothing of the car and the rocket, etc.

But the Truthful, blessed and exalted is He, completes the verse: ﴿And He creates what you do not know﴾ [An-Nahl: 8], so as to place in the Qur'an a store for every means of transport and conveyance that will be newly developed until the Day of Resurrection.

Also among this is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Glory be to Him who created all the pairs, of what the earth grows, and of themselves, and of what they do not know﴾ [Ya-Sin: 36]. Thus everything in existence is founded upon pairs, male and female, even inanimate things in which we see no life.

Among this also is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. The Romans have been defeated, in the nearest land; but they, after their defeat, will overcome, within a few years﴾ [Ar-Rum: 1-4].

Who can judge the outcome of a battle seven years in advance? Then Allah confirmed it, and the Romans prevailed, and they were People of the Book against the Persians, who worshipped fire. Therefore the Exalted said: ﴿And on that day the believers will rejoice in the victory of Allah﴾ [Ar-Rum: 4-5].

When the Companions longed to perform the 'umrah and there descended upon the Messenger of Allah the saying of the Exalted: ﴿You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills, in security, with your heads shaved and [hair] shortened, without fear. He knew what you did not know and has arranged before that a conquest near﴾ [Al-Fath: 27].

So the Messenger of Allah set out with them until they reached Hudaybiyyah, at a distance of about twenty-two kilometres from Makkah. The Quraysh confronted them and prevented them from performing the 'umrah, and they stipulated that they return the following year. They wrote a document in which they bound themselves. When the Messenger of Allah dictated to the scribe: "This is what Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, has agreed upon," 'Amr ibn Suhayl stood up and said: "If we knew that you were the Messenger of Allah we would not have fought you nor turned you back; rather, write: This is what Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah has agreed upon."

At this the Companions of the Messenger of Allah were roused and became angry, to the point that they argued with the Messenger of Allah. 'Umar said: "O Messenger of Allah, are we not upon the truth?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Are they not upon falsehood?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then why should we accept humiliation in our religion?" Al-Siddiq said: "Keep to his stirrup, O 'Umar," meaning: stand at your limit; he is the Messenger of Allah (2).

When 'Ali ibn Abi Talib insisted on writing "Muhammad the Messenger of Allah," the Messenger of Allah looked at him and said: "O 'Ali, you will be asked for something like it and you will accept it" (3). The days and years passed, and the Messenger of Allah died, then Abu Bakr, then 'Umar, then 'Uthman. When 'Ali assumed the caliphate and strife arose between him and Mu'awiyah, and the battles of the Camel and then Siffin took place between them, 'Ali was compelled to write with Mu'awiyah a document to end the fighting, and 'Ali dictated: "This is what 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Commander of the Believers, has agreed upon." They said to him: "If you were the Commander of the Believers we would not have fought you." 'Ali then recalled the saying of the Messenger of Allah: "You will be asked for something like it and you will accept it."

Thus: Allah tore away for His Messenger the veil of the past time and the future time. What then of the present time, and how does the veil of it get torn? This is seen in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And they say to themselves: Why does Allah not punish us for what we say?﴾ (Al-Mujadilah) [Allah informed him of what was in the hearts of the people].

In the expedition of Mu'tah, which is the only expedition in which the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, did not take part in person, yet it is called an expedition (ghazwah), because the term ghazwah is used only for a battle in which the Messenger of Allah took part; but at Mu'tah he witnessed it and observed it while he was in Madinah, for Allah tore away the veil of the present, so that he informed his Companions in Madinah of what was happening at Mu'tah as though he were seeing it with his own eyes.

On that day command was held by a group of senior Companions: Zayd ibn Harithah, Ibn Rawahah, Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, and Khalid ibn al-Walid. The Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, would say: "So-and-so has been killed, the banner has fallen, so-and-so has taken it, and so-and-so has been killed and carried it," and so on. When they returned from the expedition they reported exactly what the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, had reported (4).

1 'Uthman ibn 'Affan said: The Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, would receive surahs of many verses, and when something was revealed to him he would call one of those who used to write and say: "Place these verses in the surah in which such-and-such is mentioned." Related by al-Suyuti in (al-Itqan fi 'Ulum al-Qur'an 1/172).
.
2 Related by Ahmad in his Musnad (4/325, 330) within a long hadith about the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, from the narration of al-Miswar ibn Makhramah al-Zuhri and Marwan ibn al-Hakam.
3 'Ali ibn Abi Talib cited this in his argument against the Kharijites who rebelled against him and reproached him for corresponding with Mu'awiyah, and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib wrote, stripped of the title Commander of the Believers, saying: "Suhayl ibn 'Amr came to us when we were with the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, at Hudaybiyyah, when he made a treaty with his people, the Quraysh. The Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, wrote 'In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.' Suhayl said: 'I will not write "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful." How should you write?' He said: 'Write "In Your name, O Allah."' The Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, said: 'Write.' He wrote. Then he said: 'Write: This is what Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, has made peace upon.' He said: 'Had I known that you are the Messenger of Allah I would not have opposed you. Write: This is what Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah has made peace upon with Quraysh.'" (al-Bidayah wa'l-Nihayah of Ibn Kathir 7/291).
4 Related by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (4262) from the hadith of Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet, peace be upon him, announced the death of Zayd, Ja'far and Ibn Rawahah to the people before their news reached them, saying: "The banner was taken by Zayd and he was struck down; then Ja'far took it and was struck down; then Ibn Rawahah took it and was struck down" – and his eyes were shedding tears – "until the banner was taken by a sword among the swords of Allah, and Allah granted them victory."

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 28, verse 47:

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says:

{And had it not been that a calamity should afflict them for what their hands have put forward, and they should say, "Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger so we could follow Your signs and be among the believers?"} [al-Qasas 47]

The meaning: "Had it not been that a calamity should afflict them for what their hands have put forward, We would have punished them." So they would argue, saying: ﴿Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger so we could follow Your signs and be among the believers?﴾ [al-Qasas 47]. Had Allah punished them without sending a messenger to them, they would have had a proof (hujjah) against Him.

We have already said that there is no punishment without a prohibition (tajrim), no prohibition without a text (nass), and no text without notification (i'lam). Therefore, laws are published in official gazettes so that everyone may know them; the proof thus binds them, and no one is excused by ignorance of the law, nor is he exempt from punishment.

So: Allah cut off their proof when He sent to them the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with the method of truth, which guides them to good and to the reward for it in Paradise, and warns them against evil and the punishment for it in the Fire. ﴿So that people will have no argument against Allah after the messengers.﴾ [al-Nisa' 165]

So: the wisdom in sending a messenger is to establish the proof against those to whom he is sent, simply the establishment of proof; because the matters of religion are matters of innate truth (haqq fitri) which a sound intellect reaches by its natural disposition. For this reason the orientalists have paused long at the personality of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him.

They say: "You mention 'Umar in everything: in justice you say 'Umar, in strength you say 'Umar, and regarding the presence of the Messenger of Allah you say the Qur'an descended in agreement with the words of 'Umar. Do you have no one but 'Umar?"

It is as if the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, shows us through the personality of 'Umar that He, glorified is He, has not obligated us with matters from which the natural disposition recoils, but with matters which our sound disposition accepts and which it reaches by its upright nature, free of desire. 'Umar was not a prophet or a messenger, yet he reached the truth through the faith-based and sound intellectual disposition within him, free of passions, until his sound disposition led him to utter the same words the Qur'an uttered.

The phrase ﴿Had it not been... 47﴾ [al-Qasas] comes with one of two meanings: if it enters a nominal sentence, it is a particle of prohibition due to existence (harf imtina' li-wujud), as when you say: "Had it not been for Zayd with you, I would have visited you," where the visit was prevented due to the existence of Zayd. Of this type is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And had it not been that a calamity should afflict them...﴾ [al-Qasas 47], the estimate being: "Had it not been for their being afflicted."

If "law" (lawla) enters a verbal sentence, it conveys urging and exhortation, as you say to your child: "Why do you not study your lessons (lawla dhakkarta durusaka)?" Likewise the second "lawla" in the verse: ﴿they should say, "Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger so we could follow Your signs and be among the believers?"﴾ [al-Qasas 47]

Then Allah, glorified is He, says:

{So when the truth came to them from Us, they said, "Why was he not given the like of what Moses was given?" Did they not disbelieve in what Moses was given before? They said, "Two works of magic supporting each other," and they said, "Indeed, we are disbelievers in both."}

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when the truth came to them from Us...﴾ [al-Qasas: 48], that is, the Messenger whom they had asked for. ﴿They said, "Why was he not given the like of what Moses was given?"﴾ [al-Qasas: 48]. Glory be to God! "If you are a liar, then be a man of truth." You asked only for a Messenger and did not ask along with him for a specific miracle, saying: ﴿Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger...﴾ [al-Qasas: 47], and then you demand tangible signs like those with which Moses was sent before.

Whoever reflects will find that the signs before Muhammad (ﷺ) were tangible, cosmic signs, such as the ship of Noah (peace be upon him), the she-camel of Salih (peace be upon him), the staff of Moses (peace be upon him), and the healing of the blind and the leper and the raising of the dead by God's permission for our master Jesus (peace be upon him). All of these are tangible miracles that end when their time ends. They are therefore suited to messengers whose time and place were limited.

As for the Messenger who was sent to all people in time and in place, a tangible, time-bound sign does not suit him, because it would be a miracle only for its own time, and the ages after it would be left without a miracle. Therefore God, blessed and exalted is He, brought through the hand of Muhammad (ﷺ) a lasting, eternal miracle, preserved by God's preservation until the Day of Resurrection.

We have said that the messengers before Muhammad (ﷺ) would come with a miracle that confirmed the truth of their message from God, and with a book carrying their method. The book is other than the miracle. But Muhammad's (ﷺ) miracle is the very book and method with which he was sent, so that the proof of his truthfulness remains together with the method that people are required to follow. And until the Hour comes, we will keep saying: Muhammad is the Messenger of God; this is his miracle.

As for his brother messengers before him, we say "so-and-so," and his miracle was such-and-such, by way of report, and a report may be true or false.

We have affirmed all of these miracles, because God informed us of them in the noble Qur'an. So the Qur'an, which came as both miracle and method, has the merit of preserving these miracles, because it reported them and perpetuated their mention.

Then God answers them: ﴿Did they not disbelieve in what Moses was given before?﴾ [al-Qasas: 48]. Then He relates what they said about the miracle of Moses and the miracle of Muhammad: ﴿They said, "Two works of magic supporting each other"﴾ [al-Qasas: 48], that is, Moses brought magic and Muhammad brought another magic, and they ﴿supported each other﴾ [al-Qasas: 48] against us, meaning they cooperated. It is derived from "al-zahr" (back), as if you said: "Give me your back with my back, so that we may carry together," and the back is the place of load-bearing.

The reply to this accusation is easy. The miracle of Moses, although of the same genus as magic, is not magic. Magic makes you imagine that ropes are snakes slithering, whereas what Moses did was turn the staff into a real snake that moved and swallowed their magic. Therefore the magicians threw themselves down prostrate, because they saw a miracle not of the kind in which they excelled, and so they believed at once.

As for those who said of Muhammad (ﷺ) that he is a magician, the reply to them is simple: why then did he not bewitch you as well, as he bewitched those who believed in him?

Then they confirm their disbelief in both messengers, Moses and Muhammad: ﴿They said, "Indeed, we are disbelievers in both."﴾ [al-Qasas: 48]

Footnote 1: Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir (7/5181): There are three opinions on this. First: Moses and Muhammad, peace be upon them. This is the view of the Arab polytheists, and Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan said so. Second: Moses and Aaron. This is the view of the Jews toward them both at the beginning of the mission, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said so. Third: Jesus and Muhammad (ﷺ). This is the view of the Jews today, and Qatadah said so. It is also said: Did not all the Jews disbelieve in what Moses was given in the Torah concerning the mention of the Messiah, and the mention of the Gospel and the Qur'an? So they regarded Moses and Muhammad as two magicians and the two books as two sorceries.

Meaning of ﴿Say...﴾ [al-Qasas 49]: that is, in refuting them. ﴿Then bring a Book from God which is better guidance than these two...﴾ [al-Qasas 49]: that is, better guidance than the Torah that Moses brought and better than the Qur'an that Muhammad brought, since they have not satisfied you. ﴿...that I may follow it, if you are truthful﴾ [al-Qasas 49]: meaning, if you were to bring it, I would follow it.

This means there are two methods: the method of truth, which Muhammad brought, and the method of falsehood, to which they insist on holding. This challenge from our master, the Messenger of God (ﷺ), to the disbelievers means that there is no Book more rightly guided than what he brought, neither among that people nor among those who will come after them. When the Messenger of God concedes to them the possibility of a Book better than his Book, he lures them into seeking it; but when they seek it, they will not find a Book better than his, and so they will recognize the truth which the Messenger of God did not state outright. Can any human being devise for people a method better than the method of God?

So he says to them: ﴿if you are truthful﴾ [al-Qasas 49], while he knows that they are not truthful, because God Most High made Muhammad (ﷺ) the Seal of the Messengers, so no messengers will come after him, such that a messenger comes and you find fault with him and then another comes with a new Book. You will not be able to bring a Book from your own selves, because every legislator will bring the method that serves his school of thought and pleases his desires.

Therefore we say: a legislator must possess the following qualities:

First: he must have broad knowledge, such that nothing he enacts can be found lacking in the future. This is not available in any human being, as evidenced by the fact that the laws enacted in the past are no longer suitable now; people frequently call for their amendment, since new matters have arisen that were absent from the mind of the first legislator. When this matter emerged, humanity followed up with experience, and then demanded their amendment.

Second: it is required of the legislator that he have no desire regarding what he legislates for people. We see the capitalists, the communists and others each legislating in line with their own school and way of life; therefore legislation for people must not be entrusted to any of them, because none of them is free of desire.

Third: it is required of him that he not benefit from anything he legislates.

When the affairs of life and their organization necessitate that we legislate for them, then none of mankind should legislate for us except people of mature intellect and upright thought, such that they possess maturity in legislation. But until they attain maturity in legislation, what method would they follow?

If a gap occurs in legislation, people would live without law. Otherwise, who legislated for the first legislator? The one who legislated for the first legislator is the One who created the first of creation.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 28, verse 50:

Then the Truthful One, glory be to Him, says:

{ Then if they do not respond to you, know that they only follow their own desires. And who is more astray than one who follows his desire without guidance from Allah? Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people. }

This means that Allah, exalted is He, did not yield to what they wanted, so He did not send them another Book. But how would this Book have come to them? The Truthful One, blessed and exalted is He, answers this question with His saying: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not revealed to a man of importance from the two cities?﴾ [az-Zukhruf]

So, the issue for them is not the Book; it is rather the one upon whom the Book was revealed. And this is the meaning of ﴿they only follow their own desires﴾ [al-Qasas].

Then He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And who is more astray...﴾ [al-Qasas], meaning: there is none more astray ﴿than one who follows his desire without guidance from Allah﴾ [al-Qasas], that is, one who follows the desire of his own self. As for when his desire agrees with the desire of the Lawgiver, this is praiseworthy, as the Messenger of Allah explained in the noble hadith: ((None of you truly believes until his desire is subordinate to what I have brought.))(1)

In this case, we do not follow desire; we follow the Shari'ah. Therefore, one of the righteous who spent his life in obedience and worship said: "O Allah, I fear that You will not reward me for my obedience, because You commanded us to fight the desires of our souls, and I have come to love obedience so much that it has become a desire for me."

The worst of misguidance is that a person follows his desire, because desires conflict among creatures just as their goals conflict; therefore opposites in events exist in the cosmos.

Al-Mutanabbi(2) expressed this conflict, saying:
"I see that all of us seek life for ourselves,
eager for it, infatuated with it from youth.
The coward's love of self brings him to flee,
while the brave man's love of self brings him to the battle."

So we all love life and are eager for it, but our means differ. The coward, out of his love of life, flees from war, while the brave man throws himself into its turmoil even though he loves life, for he loves another life that is more lasting: the life of the martyr.

Another says:
"Everyone in existence seeks prey,
but the snares are different."

The man who gives in charity what he has, despite his need for it, has seen someone more needy than himself, and concerning him Allah says: ﴿and they prefer [others] over themselves, even though they themselves are in poverty﴾ [al-Hashr].

We say: this one preferred the poor man over himself, but from another angle he seeks reward and hopes for ten times what he spent, indeed he hopes for Paradise. So the matter has an element of utility. Religion, according to the verifiers, is self-interest, but it is an elevated, refined self-interest, not a foolish self-interest; it is that which raises its possessor, making him positive and beneficial to others, and it does not matter to him afterward that he seeks benefit for himself.

When the Shari'ah tells you: "Do not steal," and when it commands you to lower your gaze, and other commands of the Shari'ah, it only restricts your freedom as an individual, but on your behalf it restricts the freedoms of all others. It has given you more than it has taken from you, so when you look at what it took from you by following the divine method, do not forget what it gave you.
