Perhaps some conceit entered him and he relied on his own study and forgot Allah's success granted to him, so Allah wanted to teach him this lesson, to make him know that the matter in the end is in Allah's hand and by His help, and that he is the loser if this help does not reach him, in accordance with the saying of the poet:

"If there is no help from Allah for the youth,
the first thing that will be harvested from him is his striving."

So you must consider whether the calamity is the result of what you have sent forth. If so, blame no one but yourself. But if you have taken the means, and fulfilled what was required of you, and then calamity struck you, know that Allah has wisdom in it, and you must honour the wisdom of Allah and His decree in His creation.

From another perspective, calamities may be divided into two kinds: one kind in which you have an opponent, such as someone assaulting you with beating or killing or the like, and another kind in which you have no opponent, such as death and sickness, for example.

Allah, exalted and glorified, has given us a ruling for each of them. For the first type, where you have no opponent, He says, on the tongue of Luqman as he advised his son: ﴿And be patient over what has afflicted you. Indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination. 17﴾ [Luqman].

And He says concerning the case where you have an opponent: ﴿And whoever is patient and forgives—indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination. 43﴾ [al-Shura]. Since He mentioned forgiveness and called you to it, there must be an opponent before you whom you should be patient with and forgive. The opponent provokes me toward disobedience and toward retaliation, so whenever I see him I become consumed with rage. Patience in this state is more intense and requires firm resolve.

Therefore He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And whoever is patient and forgives—indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination. 43﴾ [al-Shura], and did not say, as in the first, ﴿Indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination. 17﴾ [Luqman], but rather used the emphatic form with the lam: "la-man" (whoever).

Our Lord, blessed and exalted, teaches us how to treat the rage of souls before the opponent, saying, glorified is He: ﴿Those who restrain anger and who pardon people—and Allah loves the doers of good. 134﴾ [Al 'Imran].

These are three stages, which progress you according to what readiness for good and capacity for forgiveness you have. The first is that you suppress your anger, meaning that the anger exists but you conceal it within yourself. If you rise higher, you pardon by removing the anger and rancour from your soul, as though nothing had happened. If you rise to the highest rank, you do good, for Allah loves the doers of good. Doing good means that you advance goodness and take the initiative toward the one who wronged you, making it a response to his wrong.

There is no doubt that these stages require striving; they are harsh on the soul, and few find someone who practises them. Therefore Allah did not make them obligatory; rather, He recommended and urged them. If you take the first of them, there is nothing upon you, because Allah has permitted you to return an offence with its like. If you suppress your anger, you are upon good. If you choose for yourself the ascent in obedience to your Lord, then you are an excellent man, and it is enough for you that ﴿Allah loves the doers of good. 134﴾ [Al 'Imran].

It is also sufficient for you that the one who wrongs you has, by his wrong, placed Allah on your side. Despite his wronging you, he deserves a reward from you, as one of the knowers said: "Shall I not do good to the one whom Allah has placed on my side?"

We give an example of this: a father who finds that one of his children has attacked another inclines toward the one who was attacked, showing him affection and trying to please him, until the aggressor becomes enraged and regrets having wronged his brother. Likewise, Allah, blessed and exalted, when some of His creatures wrong others, embraces the wronged and supports him against the one who wronged him.

(1) Related by Imam Ahmad in his Musnad (5/364), and Abu Dawud in his Sunan (4985), from a man among the Companions.
(2) Related by Ahmad in his Musnad (3/128, 199, 285), al-Nasa'i in his Sunan (7/61), and al-Hakim in his Mustadrak (2/160), from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him. Al-Hakim said: "Sahih according to the condition of Muslim, though they did not narrate it," and al-Dhahabi concurred. Its complete text: "Women and perfume have been made beloved to me from your world, and the coolness of my eyes has been made in prayer."
(3) From the poetry of the Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him.
(4) Abu Nu'aym related something similar from a hadith of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud in al-Hilya (4/237), and Ibn al-Jawzi with his chain in al-'Ilal al-Mutanahiya (2/519) and declared it weak. Al-'Ajluni cited it in Kashf al-Khafa (1/457).

Then Qarun is suddenly seized by the punishment he deserved:

{So We caused the earth to swallow him and his home. He had no company to help him against Allah, nor was he among those who could defend themselves.} (81)

Al-khasf (the sinking into the earth): that the earth is split open and swallows what is upon it, like one who says, "O earth, split open and swallow me." The sinking happened to him and to his home, in which were his treasures, his storehouses, and all that he possessed. ﴿So he had no company to help him against Allah.﴾ [al-Qasas: 81] Wealth did not benefit him, and no people of his defended him. ﴿Nor was he among those who could defend themselves﴾ [al-Qasas: 81], meaning: by his own self. He had no band to protect him, and he could not protect himself. So who can repel the punishment of Allah if it descends, and who can prevent it or carry it out if the earth swallows him up?!

Here we should ask: what is now the state of those who were deceived by him, and were seduced by his wealth and adornment?

{ And those who had wished to be in his place the day before began to say: "Woe! It is Allah who extends provision to whom He wills of His servants and restricts it. Had Allah not been gracious to us, He would have caused the earth to swallow us up. Woe! The disbelievers will not prosper." }

Yesterday they were saying, "Oh, would that we had like what Qarun was given" (Qur'an 28:79). But today, after they had witnessed what befell him of Allah's punishment and His might, which is not turned back from the disbelieving people, they return to their senses and say: "Woe! It is Allah who extends provision to whom He wills of His servants and restricts it" (Qur'an 28:82).

The word "wai" (وي) is a verb-like interjection, like "uff" (أف) and "hayhat" (هيهات), and it expresses regret and grief over what one has done. It is a reproach and self-blame for the act. It may also be used to express wonder. So their saying "wai" was a expression of remorse for their wish for the blessing with which Qarun had been favoured, and a self-reproach, after they had seen him and his dwelling swallowed up. Now they regret and blame themselves, because Allah the Exalted has wisdom and decree in His provision.

"Yabsutu al-rizqa li-man yasha'u min 'ibadihi wa yaqdir" (Qur'an 28:82) means: He withholds and constricts. Extending provision is not a sign of honour, nor is restricting it a sign of humiliation, as evidenced by the fact that Allah extended provision to Qarun and then seized him, the Mighty, the Omnipotent.

Surah al-Fajr addressed this matter in His saying: "As for man, when his Lord tests him and honours him and blesses him, he says, 'My Lord has honoured me.' But when He tests him and restricts his provision, he says, 'My Lord has humiliated me'" (Qur'an 89:15-16).

The first considered abundant provision a sign of honour, and the second considered restriction a sign of humiliation. So the Exalted corrected this view, saying: "No!" (Qur'an 89:17). That is, you are both mistaken: neither abundance of provision is a sign of honour, nor restriction a sign of humiliation. Otherwise, how could the giving of wealth be a sign of honour, when I give some people wealth and they do not fulfil Allah's right in it?

"No! Rather, you do not honour the orphan (17). Nor do you urge one another to feed the poor (18). And you devour inheritance, devouring greedily (19). And you love wealth with abundant love (20)" (Qur'an 89:17-20).

So what honour is there in wealth that becomes a burden upon its owner and a trial in which he is not granted success? Had this wealth been taken from its owner, it would have been better for him. This wealth is like a weapon in the hand of one who does not know how to use it, who may kill himself with it.

His saying, "Had Allah not been gracious to us, He would have caused the earth to swallow us up" (Qur'an 28:82), is because yesterday they wished to be in his place; but now they acknowledge that Allah has been gracious to them in saving them from that fate. Then they say, "Woe! The disbelievers will not prosper" (Qur'an 28:82), an expression of wonder that the disbelievers do not prosper in the sight of Allah the Exalted.

Thereafter, the Exalted One brings a general principle to settle this matter:

{ That is the abode of the Hereafter. We grant it to those who do not desire exaltation upon the earth, nor corruption, and the good end is for the righteous. (83) }

For it is not proper for a human being to exalt himself over his fellow creatures or over his environment except by something intrinsic to him. He cannot exalt himself by his strength, for he may fall ill and become weak; nor by his wealth, for it may be taken from him.

So then: beware of exalting yourself over others by something that was bestowed upon you. If you wish, let it be by something intrinsic in you. But there is nothing intrinsic in you; you are no better than anyone, so that you could rise above him. Moreover, the world is subject to change, and what you possess may pass to them. Would it please you, if your neighbour became rich or strong, that he should look down on you?

Furthermore, you cannot rise except by relying on a power higher than you that supports you. Try it yourself: attempt to leap upward like the acrobat in the circus, then hold yourself up in that height. Of course you will not be able to, and why? Because you have no intrinsic self-sufficiency in height.

Since this is the case, beware of exalting yourself, for by your exaltation you diminish others; and if the opposite happens, they will revile you. Also, a person does not rise above his environment or his place unless he sees everyone around him beneath him. When you see that all people are beneath you, you have not become aware of the secrets of God's grace in His creation.

Were you to reflect, you would find in each of them a quality that you do not have. And if you consider that all people are the dependents and creatures of God, that none of us has a kinship or relationship with God that sets him apart, and that we are all equal before Him, the Exalted, and He has distributed gifts among us all equally, so that no one is distinguished above another, then why exaltation? And why pride?

Also, the one who exalts himself does so only in heedlessness of the greatness of his Lord's majesty. Whoever keeps in mind the greatness and majesty of his Lord must be humble, must shrink before His majesty, the Exalted, and must be ashamed to be proud over His creatures.

The Prophet (ﷺ) teaches us how to respect others and how to be humble toward them. When the noble companion 'Adi ibn Hatim(1) entered upon him, he rose from his seat out of honour for him; that is, if he was sitting on a cushion, for example, he would get up from it and give it to his companion so that he might sit upon it.

Thus the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was keen on equality in the assembly. Therefore 'Adi ibn Hatim said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "I bear witness that you do not desire exaltation upon the earth, and I bear witness that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God," and he embraced Islam.

How strange is what we see, for example, in our mosques, which are the houses of God and the places most worthy of this equality. You see that when one of the influential people enters, they spread a prayer mat for him to pray upon, even though the mosque is already carpeted, to the highest standard of cleanliness. Why this discrimination?

Yet we find among them one who moves this prayer mat aside and prays as the rest of the people pray. I think that the one who accepts to have this prayer mat placed for him is, I believe, seeking exaltation upon the earth.

The Exalted One wills for the human being to live in balanced movement among balanced people, so that hearts remain harmonious, with no rancour entering them; and when hearts are free of rancour, a single loaf of bread is enough for all people.

Then He, the Exalted, says: {and the good end is for the righteous (83)} — that is, the good outcome, and the excellent end, which is everlasting enduring bliss, is for the righteous.

1 He is Ibn Hatim al-Ta'i, famous for generosity. 'Adi embraced Islam in the ninth year, and it is said in the tenth year. He had been a Christian before that, and he remained steadfast in his Islam when some Arabs apostatised after the death of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). He witnessed the conquests of Iraq, then settled in Kufa, witnessed Siffin with 'Ali, and died after the year sixty AH. [Al-Isaba fi Tamyiz al-Sahaba by Ibn Hajar (biography no. 5467)].

Then the Truthful Lord says:

{Whoever comes with a good deed, he will have better than it, and whoever comes with an evil deed, those who did evil deeds will not be recompensed except according to what they used to do.} (28:84)

We have said that the word (khayr) is used to mean the opposite of evil, as in His saying: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it. And whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it.﴾ (99:7-8)

It is also used to mean "better" within the category of good. You say: "This is better than that," for both of them contain good. From this is the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "The strong believer is better (khayr) and more beloved to Allah than the weak believer, and there is good in each." It is then in the sense of comparison, meaning: "more excellent than it." From this is the poet's saying:

Zayd is the best (khiyar) of people, and the son of the best (al-akhyar)

Here he used the comparative form according to the original usage. You say: "This is good (hasan), and that is better (ahsan)."

So the meaning here, ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed, he will have better than it..﴾ (28:84), is: there comes to him good from its direction, or, when he does good, Allah gives him something better and more excellent than it. The intended meaning is that a good deed is rewarded tenfold.

The Truthful Lord gives us an illustrative image of this matter, saying: ﴿The example of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah is like a grain that grows seven spikes, in each spike a hundred grains. And Allah multiplies for whom He wills, and Allah is All-Encompassing and Knowing.﴾ (2:261)

His saying ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed..﴾ (28:84) is a matter of creed, establishing and affirming reward for the obedient and punishment for the disobedient. The meaning of ﴿comes with a good deed..﴾ (28:84) is: he brings it as a new event that did not exist before. When you perform a good deed, you have brought it into existence by means of the power to obey and the capacity to do good that Allah placed in you.

Or the meaning is: he brings the good deed to Allah as something better, so that he may obtain its reward, and there is no obstacle to these acts of coming all gathering for him so that he approaches Allah with them, and He recompenses him for them in the Hereafter.

But is the reward of a good deed restricted only to the Hereafter, or did the religion with its matters come for the happiness of this world and the happiness of the Hereafter? Since the religion is for the happiness of both abodes, the good deed has an effect in this world too, but its full sum is yours in the Hereafter.

This verse came after the discussion of Qarun, and after his people advised him, and their advice included: ﴿And do good as Allah has done good to you..﴾ (28:77). So their request that he do good as Allah has done good to him came in the context of mentioning good deeds. Is "good" that which a person finds pleasant? No, because a person may find a thing pleasant and it brings him harm, and he may dislike a thing and not find it pleasant, yet it brings him benefit.

So who determines good and evil? Since people differ on this matter, none determines it except Allah, Who created people and knows what suits them. He is the One who knows the properties of things and the consequences that follow from them. As for man, Allah created him fit for good and fit for evil; he does what is good and does what is ugly, and matters may become confused for him.

Therefore they define good as: what the Shari'ah has deemed good, not what you deem good. For example, we find some foods palatable and find in them enjoyment and pleasure, although they are harmful, while we disdain, for instance, eating boiled food, although it is more beneficial and useful. Therefore He says regarding food: ﴿So eat it, with satisfaction and wholesomeness.﴾ (4:4), because food may be pleasant, so you find enjoyment in it, but it is not wholesome (marī'), and it causes you troubles afterward.

The Truthful Lord says here: ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed, he will have better than it..﴾ (28:84). So the good deed is good, but the reward for it is better than it, i.e., more excellent; because it is a constant, lasting gift that does not end, or it is good that comes to you because of it. As the people of riddles and wordplay say: "Muhammad is better (khayr) than his Lord," meaning: good that reaches us from Allah. There is no need for such riddles when they allow an unacceptable meaning.

Then He says: ﴿Whoever comes with an evil deed..﴾ (28:84). The Truthful Lord did not say: "then he will have worse than it," by analogy with the good deed, so that the evil deed would be multiplied as We multiplied the good deed. This matter is a manifestation of Allah's mercy toward His creation, a mercy that extends even to the disobedient among His creatures.

Therefore He said: ﴿So those who did evil deeds will not be recompensed except according to what they used to do.﴾ (28:84), i.e., in proportion to it, without increase.

If you wish, read His saying in Surat (Amma): ﴿Indeed, for the righteous is a place of attainment: gardens and grapevines, and full-breasted [companions] of equal age, and a full cup. They hear therein no ill speech or lying. Reward from your Lord, a gift [and] account (hisaban).﴾ (78:31-36). So "hisaban" here does not mean that the reward is by reckoning according to the amount of deed; rather it means sufficient for them in every aspect of good, and from it our saying: "Hasbi Allah," meaning: Allah is sufficient for me.

On the other side, regarding evil deeds, He says: ﴿A recompense in accordance (wifaqan).﴾ (78:26), i.e., according to its measure, corresponding to it.

Thus our Lord, Mighty and Majestic, treats us with bounty rather than strict justice, to encourage people to do good. When you do a good deed, you are one who presents your good deed to all people, and in return the effect of the good deeds of the masses all returns to you; you receive from each one of them a good deed, as if it were a "sale" (auction) of good deeds returning to you.

[1] Narrated by Ahmad ibn Hanbal in his Musnad (2/366, 37), and likewise Muslim in his Sahih (2664) and Ibn Majah in his Sunan (79), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him).

[2] Al-kawa'ib al-atrab: i.e., maidens mature and of equal age. Ka'b al-thady: the breast's protrusion and swelling; a girl is called ka'ib, i.e., one with a prominent breast. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/164].

[3] Al-ka's al-dihaq: the full cup, continuously filled for its drinkers. His saying ﴿and a full cup﴾ (78:34) means: it is a constant fullness, and this is a metaphor for lasting bliss. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/234].

Then Allah, glory be to Him, says to His Prophet:

{Indeed, the One who imposed the Qur'an upon you will surely bring you back to a return. Say: My Lord knows best who has come with guidance and who is in manifest error.} (28:85)

The meaning of *fard* (imposed, obligated): to oblige, to make binding, to decree. The root meaning of *fard* is to cut or sever. When you cut something with a knife, for example, it is called *fard*, because it has come out of its natural form. Likewise, the Qur'an takes the self out of its natural inclination, cuts off its own will, and returns it to the will of Allah. For this reason, He, glory be to Him, says at the beginning of Surat al-Nur: ﴿A surah which We have sent down and imposed⁠﴾ (24:1).

That is, We have made it certain and binding upon you. Obligation means returning the self to what its Creator wants from it, regardless of what it itself desires. He may command it to do what it dislikes and forbid it from what it loves. Thus, it cuts off the flow of the self's desires, because the self is usually one that commands to evil, looks to the immediate, does not care for the future, and does not reckon for it.

The Qur'an is Allah's method: "do" and "do not do." It is what restrains the self's unruliness and defines the limits of its will, because the Creator, Mighty and Majestic, created the self and made its will capable of doing good and of doing evil.

We have previously discussed the difference between *ibad* (worshippers who choose devotion) and *abid* (slaves), and we said: all creation is a slave of Allah, believer and disbeliever alike. Even if the disbeliever refuses Allah regarding faith, he is subjugated to Him, exalted is He, in other matters, such as illness, death, and other things. Then Allah gave us a sphere of choice, so that He may reward whoever deserves reward and punish whoever deserves punishment, justly.

When the sensible person sees that he is subjugated to Allah in matters of decree from which he cannot escape, and over which he has no control, he relinquishes his own desire and his own choice in favor of his Lord's desire and his Lord's choice, and he is content to be directed in everything. At this point, they move from being slaves to being worshippers.

So the *ibad* are those who give up the choices granted to them by Allah in favor of Allah's will in judgment. By this logic, everyone in the Hereafter will be a slave, because they will have no choice, and the believer and the disbeliever will be equal in that, on the Day when He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿To whom belongs the dominion this Day? To Allah, the One, the Subduer⁠﴾ (40:16).

The sending down of the Qur'an is called *fard* because of the obligations it contains, which are usually hard on the self. Do you not see His saying, exalted is He, about prayer, which is the mother of acts of worship: ﴿And indeed, it is a great burden except for the humble⁠﴾ (2:45).

No one recognizes its rank and status except the humble. For this reason, the Prophet ﷺ used to say to Bilal: "Give us rest with it, O Bilal." And he said: "The coolness of my eye has been placed in prayer." Because he ﷺ loved it and was passionate about it, until it became the coolness of his eye and the ultimate source of his rest.

Thus, when an obligation is first imposed, it must be difficult. Therefore, it requires firmness of faith and steadfastness of certainty, such that you trust that the difficult work upon you now will bring you good and lasting happiness in the Hereafter.

And He, exalted is He, says about fighting: ﴿Fighting has been enjoined upon you while it is hateful to you⁠﴾ (2:216). There is no doubt that it is repugnant to the self. But if you keep in mind the reward, and you know that it is either victory or martyrdom, then it will become sweet to you until you love it, and you hasten toward it yourself. Like the Companion at Badr, when he heard what the martyr receives in reward, and he had a date in his mouth that he was chewing, and he said: "Is there not between me and Paradise only that I fight and be killed?" Then he threw away the date and hurried to the battlefield.

Therefore, Allah, glory be to Him, magnifies the rewards in the heart of the believer, so that he may approach the work with love and desire. From here, some of the knowers who have loved goodness until it has become a desire of the self for them say: "I fear that Allah will not reward me for obedience." Why? He says: "Because I have come to desire it," i.e., just as the people of disobedience desire disobedience.

When faith brings its possessor to the level where he loves obedience, he has become a devoted servant (*rabbani*), who trusts in what is with Allah of reward.

The Prophet ﷺ used to stand in prayer through the night until his feet swelled. When Sayyida 'A'isha asked him: "Has not your Lord forgiven you your past and future sins?" He said: "Shall I not be a grateful servant?"

The meaning of ﴿to return you to a return⁠﴾ (28:85): that He will repay you with the best reward. This verse was revealed when the people of Makkah persecuted the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and harmed him, until they forced him to go to al-Ta'if to seek a supporter there. But they were no less harsh than the people of Makkah, so the Messenger of Allah found no supporter there, and he returned dejected and grieved, finding no one who would grant him protection, until Mut'im ibn 'Adi granted him protection.

Consider this: when the Messenger of Allah, with his lofty status, could not find anyone to support him or grant him protection. As for the Companions, they had no power yet, nor any strength to protect the Messenger of Allah. During this period they suffered hardships in the path of the call. The disbelievers besieged them in the Shi'b of Abu Talib, and imposed a complete boycott upon them, isolating them from the people, forbidding them food and drink, buying and selling, even marriage, until they were forced to eat refuse and tree leaves.

For this reason, Allah commanded them to emigrate (*hijrah*). Emigration is either to a land of safety or to a land of faith. The emigration to a land of safety was like the emigration to Abyssinia, where the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, explaining the reason for emigrating there, said to them: "In it there is a king under whom no one is wronged." That is, al-Najashi, the king of Abyssinia. Indeed, what the Messenger of Allah said about him proved true. When Quraysh sent after them someone to speak with al-Najashi about their return and sending them back to Makkah, he refused to hand them over and to allow Quraysh access to them, even though Quraysh's gifts were great and the inducement was considerable.

This shows the greatness of the Messenger of Allah, his broad insight, and his study of the map around him, and his knowledge of who was suitable as a place of emigration for his Companions. His choice of the king of Abyssinia could only have come either by inspiration from Allah or by great intelligence, and he was an unlettered man among an unlettered people. And if the Quraysh delegation had not gone out seeking the emigrants, we would not have seen the evidence of the truth of the Messenger of Allah's words.

As a result of "no one is wronged under him," Allah honored him with Islam. He embraced Islam, and the Messenger of Allah authorized him to marry Sayyida Umm Habiba bint Abi Sufyan on his behalf. She, may Allah be pleased with her, was among the earliest emigrants to Abyssinia with her husband, who had converted to Christianity there, but she remained upon her religion and held firmly to her creed.

In this there is, first, evidence of the extent of the harm that believers suffered from the disbelievers. Second, evidence of conscious obedience in marriage: she chose to leave with her husband not out of love for him or infatuation with him, but to flee with him while preserving her religion. Therefore, when he became a Christian, she did not hesitate to leave him. Hence the Messenger of Allah asked for her for himself. Then, when al-Najashi died, the Messenger of Allah prayed over him and invoked mercy upon him. This is the emigration of faith to a land of safety.

Then emigration took place afterward to a land of faith, to Madinah, after the First and Second Pledges of al-'Aqabah, and after the Messenger of Allah found helpers (*Ansar*) who would bear with him the burdens of the call. The Ansar in Madinah set the most wonderful example of sacrifice, one without parallel in human history.

For a man is most jealous of his wife, and does not grudge others what he owns. Would he lend you his car to ride, his house to live in, or his garment to wear and adorn himself with? But his wife remains protected, and no one dares to look at her.

Yet the Ansar had a different view on this matter, for they shared everything with their Muhajir brothers, even their wives. They considered their emigrants' departure from their families and homelands, and their estrangement, and their need and desire for women.

So one of them would say to his brother: "Look at my wives. Whichever of them pleases you, I will divorce her, and you may marry her." This is a sacrifice for which we find no parallel in the history of humanity, even among the disbelievers.

Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded emigration to Madinah. He left secretly, whereas 'Umar, for example, left openly and publicly, to the extent that he stood calling out to the people of Makkah at the top of his voice, challenging them upon his departure: "Whoever wishes that his mother be bereaved, his child orphaned, or his wife widowed, let him meet me behind this valley."

As for the Messenger of Allah, he left secretly. Some people pause at this matter, or the wisdom in it escapes them. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was always an example for the weak, whereas the strong need no one's protection and have no reason to leave openly. For this reason, no one should be ashamed to conceal themselves as the Messenger of Allah did.

Moreover, when you reflect: yes, the Messenger of Allah left secretly, but it was a secrecy of defiance. He went out from among their young men who lay in wait for him, and he scattered dust upon their faces, saying: "May the faces be disfigured."

Nevertheless, Allah's support for him did not prevent him from taking the means of deliverance, so he changed the route, because the disbelievers of Makkah knew that his destination was Madinah, since he had concluded the pledge of al-'Aqabah with the Ansar. Therefore, they lay in wait for him on that route, sent spies to search for him, and set a reward for whoever would bring him to them, ﷺ.

Whoever reflects on the event of the emigration finds that it was a well-planned strategy that took every aspect of the situation into account, as though Allah, exalted is He, wanted to teach us through the person of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ not to neglect the means and not to clash with reality as long as we are able to do so.

When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ left Makkah, which was his homeland and the land most beloved to his heart, he said: "O Allah, You have expelled me from the land most beloved to me, so settle me in the land most beloved to You."

Therefore, if Makkah was beloved to the Messenger of Allah, Madinah is beloved to Allah. For this reason, after the Messenger of Allah had left Makkah and approached Madinah, his heart yearned for Makkah, and his Lord reassured him with this verse: ﴿Indeed, the One who imposed the Qur'an upon you will surely bring you back to a return⁠﴾ (28:85).

The One who imposed upon you the hardship of obligations, and bore upon you the hardships of the call, of persuading people to it, and of implementing its rulings, He is the One who will return you to your land, as a return of victory and a return of conquest. And the return of the Messenger of Allah to his land is comparable to the return of Musa, peace be upon him, to his mother, in His saying, exalted is He, to the mother of Musa: ﴿We will surely return him to you⁠﴾ (28:7). It was not an ordinary return, but ﴿and We will make him one of the messengers⁠﴾ (28:7).

Therefore: He will return your son to you, but he will return as a victorious messenger. And just as Allah was true in the return of Musa, so He will be true in the return of Muhammad.

The meaning of ﴿*ma'ad*⁠﴾ (28:85) is not "appointment," as some assume. Rather, it means the place to which you return after leaving it, so the meaning is: We will return you to the place you yearn for, and to which your heart is attached.

Or: We will return you to a "*ma'ad*," i.e., to Us, as He said, exalted is He: ﴿So whether We show you some of what We promise them, or We take you in death, to Us they will be returned⁠﴾ (40:77). There is no objection to intending both meanings together.

Then He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿Say: My Lord knows best who has come with guidance and who is in manifest error⁠﴾ (28:85). Allah, Blessed and Exalted, teaches His Messenger Muhammad ﷺ gentle argument, not harsh argument. He teaches him how to respond to what they said about the one who believes in him: "So-and-so has apostatized (*sabā*)," meaning he has left the religion of his fathers, while they believe it to be the truth. So in their view, the one who believes has departed from the truth into falsehood.

So these are minds that need diplomacy and argument, as He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿And argue with them in the best manner⁠﴾ (16:125). Harsh argument increases your opponent in obstinacy and stubbornness, whereas gentle argument wins hearts and inclines them toward you. Therefore, the Messenger of Allah responds with His saying: ﴿Say: My Lord knows best who has come with guidance and who is in manifest error⁠﴾ (28:85). That is: the one who has come with guidance from Allah, namely the Prophet ﷺ, and ﴿who is in manifest error⁠﴾ (28:85).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 28, verse 86:

Then the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, gives His Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, a proof drawn from the reality of his own life, so that he may be reassured that he is supported by his Lord, that He, glory be to Him, will fulfil what He has promised him, that He will not abandon him, and how He would choose him for the message only to abandon him afterwards?

﴿And you did not expect that the Book would be delivered to you, except as a mercy from your Lord. So do not be at all a supporter of the disbelievers.﴾ [28:86]

That is: if you are surprised, or consider it unlikely, that We would return you to your homeland, because the disbelievers lie in wait for you, to the point that you could no longer believe you would return to it, then look at the origin of the message with you: did you think, or did your ambition aspire, to be a messenger? It was a matter that had not been in your mind, and yet Allah gave it to you and chose you for it. So the One who gave you the message, though it had not been in your mind, how would He deprive you of a matter that you love and long for?

Thus this verse serves as the proof and demonstration of the truth of ﴿Surely He who has ordained the Qur'an for you will bring you back to a place of return﴾ [28:85]. In another place the Truth, glory be to Him, affirms this same meaning, saying: ﴿And thus We have revealed to you an inspired Spirit of Our command. You did not know what the Book was, nor what faith was, but We made it a light by which We guide whom We will of Our servants.﴾ [42:52] So the One who gave you the message is not unable to fulfil for you what you desire.

As for His saying, ﴿except as a mercy from your Lord﴾ [28:86], this is an exception that they call an exception of disconnection (istithna' munqati').

The meaning is: you did not expect that the Book would be cast to you; rather, We cast it, and We cast it to you only as a mercy to you from your Lord.

Since these disbelievers have opposed you and expelled you, beware of softening towards them: ﴿So do not be at all a supporter of the disbelievers﴾ [28:86], that is, a helper or aide to them. They had proposed to the Messenger of Allah that he worship their gods for a year and they would worship his God for a year.(1) So Allah warned him against assisting them in their misguidance or going along with their falsehood. For this reason the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, never supported a wrongdoer or a criminal, even if he was one of his own followers.

We have already mentioned, in the interpretation of His saying, ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book in truth, that you may judge between people by what Allah has shown you. And do not be a advocate for the treacherous﴾ [4:105], the story of the Jews of Zayd ibn al-Simin, when the Muslim Ta'mah ibn Ubayriq came to him and deposited with him a coat of mail that was his. This coat of mail had been stolen from another man named Qatadah ibn al-Nu'man. When Qatadah missed it, he searched for it until he found it in the house of the Jew, for the thief had placed it in a bag of flour, and the trace of the flour indicated the place of the coat of mail. They accused the Jew of the theft. When they realised the true situation, they feared that the Jew would prevail over the Muslim, especially as they were recent converts to Islam, eager that his image not be marred.

Therefore they explained this matter to the Messenger of Allah, hoping he would find a way out of it. The Messenger of Allah turned the matter over in his mind before giving a ruling on it. Then the revelation descended upon the Messenger of Allah: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book in truth, that you may judge between people...﴾ [4:105], that is, all people, believer and disbeliever, ﴿by what Allah has shown you. And do not be an advocate for the treacherous﴾ [4:105], that is, do not dispute on their behalf or for their benefit. ﴿And seek forgiveness of Allah; indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [4:106], that is, for what occurred to your mind in this matter.

In some verses there appears in the outward wording a severity towards the Messenger of Allah and harshness, such as: ﴿And if he had attributed to Us some sayings, We would have seized him by the right hand, then We would have cut from him the aorta﴾ [69:44-46].

Everything in the Qur'an of this kind is not directed at our master, the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Rather, the Truth, glory be to Him, intends to give the Ummah a model that draws their attention, as if He, exalted is He, were saying to us: take heed. If the address to the Messenger of Allah is in this manner, how then is the address to you?

It is like a man who has a servant who meddles with things around him, so you address your son: "By Allah, if you meddle with anything, I will do such-and-such to you," so the reproach is directed at the son while you mean the servant, in accordance with the proverb: "It is you I mean, but listen, neighbour."

For this reason one of the knowers says:
"Whatever warning is in the Qur'an addressed to the Prophet, the bearer of glad tidings,
So be discerning and understand the allusion:
It is you I mean, but listen, neighbour."
That is: listen, O community of Muhammad, to how I address him and direct the warning to him, although he is the bringer of good news.

(1) From Ibn Abbas: the Quraysh invited the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to accept wealth from them so that he would be the richest man in Makkah, and they would marry him to whatever women he wished. They said: "This is what we offer you, Muhammad, and cease reviling our gods and do not mention our gods with evil. If you do not do so, we offer you one thing which holds benefit for you." He said: "What is it?" They said: "You worship our gods for a year, and we will worship your God for a year." He said: "Until I see what comes to me from my Lord." Then the revelation came from Allah: ﴿Say: O disbelievers, I do not worship what you worship﴾ [109:1-2]. Recorded by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur (attributing it to Ibn Jarir al-Tabari, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani).

(2) Recorded by al-Wahidi al-Nisaburi in Asbab al-Nuzul (p. 103), who said: "This is the view of a group of exegetes."

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 28, verse 88:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not invoke with Allah another deity. There is no deity except Him.﴾ [al-Qasas 88] is like the preceding verse, because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is not someone likely to invoke another deity alongside Allah. ﴿There is no deity except Him﴾ [al-Qasas 88], meaning: there is no worshipped one in truth except Him.

Had there been other deities with Him, they would have confronted Him: ﴿Say: If there were with Him other gods, as they say, they would have sought a way to the Owner of the Throne﴾ [al-Isra 42], meaning: they would have striven toward Him to contend with Him for divinity, or to draw near to Him.

﴿Everything is perishing except His Face﴾ [al-Qasas 88]. The "face" in our usage is that by which a person is confronted. Every attribute by which Allah describes Himself, we must describe Him by it, on the basis of His description within the framework of His saying: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ [al-Shura 11].

So Allah has a Face, but not like all faces, and likewise in every attribute that Allah shares in name with creation. You have believed in the existence of Allah, and that His existence is essential, not like your existence.

As for His saying: ﴿everything [shay'] [al-Qasas 88]: the word shay' (thing), they say, is the genus of genera, meaning that any existent upon which existence has come is called "thing" (shay'), however trivial and insignificant it may be. The scholars have discussed whether it may be applied to Allah, the Exalted, as "thing" because He exists.

They said: we examine the root of the word shay' (thing): it is from "one who wills something" (man yashaa shay'an), so the shay' is that which another has willed, and so brought into being. Therefore, "thing" is not said of Allah, because no one has willed Him; rather He, Glorified is He, exists by His own essence.

In another verse, Allah speaks of the generality of "thing": ﴿And there is not a thing except that it exalts His praise﴾ [al-Isra 44], meaning: everything that is called a thing is an existent whose existence was preceded by non-existence, and it glorifies the praise of Allah. Some said this is glorification as an indication of its Originator, not an actual spoken glorification. But His saying: ﴿but you do not understand their glorification﴾ [al-Isra 44] indicates that it is actual glorification, so every thing glorifies in its own language and in what suits it.

Allah has established speech for the birds and glorification for the mountains. Had you understood the language of these things, you could have come to know their glorification. But how can we hope to know the languages of stone and tree, when we do not understand the languages of one another? If you do not know English, for example, do you know what its speaker says when he glorifies Allah in it, though he is a human like you, speaking in your manner and with the same sounds?

Therefore they say about the miracles of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "The pebbles glorified in his hand." The correct statement is: the Messenger of Allah heard the glorification of the pebbles in his hand; otherwise the pebbles were glorifying in the hand of the Messenger of Allah, and glorifying in the hand of Abu Jahl. Likewise the lament of the trunk for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Then did not the Truthful Lord say: ﴿And your Lord inspired the bee﴾ [al-Nahl 68]?

Did He not say of the earth: ﴿because your Lord has inspired it﴾ [al-Zalzala 5]? Did He not establish speech for the ant? Did the hoopoe not speak to Solomon, peace be upon him, and did Solomon not understand from it?

So, every genus of creatures has its language, which its individuals understand from one another: ﴿each has known its prayer and its glorification﴾ [al-Nur 41]. And if Allah wills, He informs some of His creatures of these languages and makes them understand them.

As for the meaning of ﴿perishing [halik]﴾ [al-Qasas 88]: some think that perishing is specific to what has a soul, such as humans and animals. But if we stop at His saying: ﴿that whoever perishes might perish upon clear evidence and whoever lives might live upon clear evidence﴾ [al-Anfal 42].

So perishing is opposed by life, and every thing that perishes had a life suited to it, even if we only understand our own life, which departs with the departure of the soul.

As for the meaning of ﴿except His Face﴾ [al-Qasas 88]: that is, except His Essence, Exalted is He. He did not say "except Him," because He, Exalted, is not a thing; and the "face" here has another meaning, as we say: "I did that seeking the Face of Allah," meaning: I did it while Allah was in my mind. So the meaning is: everything perishes except what was for the Face of Allah, which never perishes, because it remains for you, and you attain its good in this world and its reward in the Hereafter.

Then He, Glorified is He, says: ﴿To Him belongs the judgment, and to Him you will be returned﴾ [al-Qasas 88], meaning: to Him belongs the judgment in the Hereafter, on the day He says: ﴿To whom belongs the dominion today?﴾ [Ghafir 16]. But why was dominion specified for the Day of Resurrection, when He, Glorified is He, has permanent dominion in this world and the Hereafter? They said: because there is a kind of dominion in this world which He grants to His creatures, as He said of Nimrod: ﴿that Allah had given him the kingdom﴾ [al-Baqara 258], and He said: ﴿You give dominion to whom You will and You remove dominion from whom You will﴾ [Al 'Imran 26].

So dominion is the dominion of Allah, and He, Glorified is He, is the One who holds dominion over His creatures in the world of causes; but in the Hereafter, ownership is stripped from anyone except Allah alone. Even the will of a person over his limbs is taken from him, so they testify against him concerning what he did in the world.

If you wish to know now the truth of this matter, look at the matters of destiny that befall you, such as illness and death and others: can you refuse them?

Then He, Glorified is He, says: ﴿and to Him you will be returned﴾ [al-Qasas 88], meaning: for reckoning in the Hereafter, because Allah, the Exalted, did not create us in vain, nor will He leave us neglected; rather there must be a return to Him to call each of you to account for what he sent forward. Since you have known this, you must respect the return to Allah and look at what He has required of you.

Whoever follows this verb in the Qur'an finds that it came once in the passive voice (turja'un, "you are returned"), and that is for the disbeliever who was arrogant toward Allah: we say to him, you will be returned to Allah, and cast into the Fire in anger from Him and in spite of your nose; if you were arrogant toward Allah in this world, you will not be arrogant toward Him in the Hereafter. And it comes in the active voice (tarji'un, "you return") for the believer who longs for the reward of the Hereafter, so he hastens with his soul and advances toward it.
